THREATS: Commercial and non-commercial fishing for hāpuʻupuʻu continue today, though rarely targeted directly and making up a relatively small proportion of the total catch of either. Though Deep-7 as a complex have been found to be neither overfished nor experiencing overfishing, health of the MHI population of hāpuʻupuʻu remains unknown. Because the species is relatively long-lived and sequentially hermaphroditic, potential negative impacts of intense fishing may be amplified.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The main Hawaiian Island (MHI) Deep-7 bottomfish complex is actively managed through a partnership between the State of Hawai'i, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council (WesPac). Management of the complex is in accordance with the Magnussen-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (MSA) which identifies the complex as Management Unit Species (MUS). Regulatory measures in place include in Annual Catch Limit for the combined Deep-7 bottomfish complex, mandatory bottomfish vessel registration, and a non-commercial daily bag limit of five fish per person, per day.
MONITORING: Benchmark stock assessments of the complex occur at five-year intervals, with an update assessment occurring in between. Data collection to inform the stock assessments is primarily fishery-dependent with fishery independent surveys in the past yielding limited information on the species.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

Research priorities today revolve primarily around improving understanding of the ecology and biology of hāpuʻupuʻu in the MHI to better inform stock assessment and future management strategies. Achieving better understanding of the State's non-commercial bottomfish fishery, which is not required to report catch, is also an area of focus. 

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

The oceanic whitetip shark is known for their unique white-mottled markings at the tips of their dorsal (top), pectoral (side), and caudal (tail) fins. They get up to 13 ft in length. They are a top predator species, but are opportunistic feeders, meaning they feed on various prey and often eat what's available. Their typical diet consists of bony fish and cephalopods such as squid, cuttlefish, and octopus. They have also been seen foraging on large pelagic game fish, like tuna, and prey on sea birds, sharks and rays, marine mammals. Oceanic whitetips live up to 25 years. They give birth every other year to a litter of pups ranging from one to 14.

## DISTRIBUTION:

The oceanic whitetip shark (Carcharhinus longimanus) is usually found offshore in the open waters of all tropical oceans worldwide. It can be confused with the whitetip reef shark (Triaenodon obesus), which is found in shallow waters around reefs.

## ABUNDANCE:

In 2018, the oceanic whitetip was listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The International Union for Conservation Nature (IUCN) lists them globally as critically endangered, meaning they face an extremely high risk of extinction. It is known that their populations have dramatically declined due to bycatch in commercial fisheries combined with the rise in demand for shark fins internationally. Globally, there is not much research currently available, however, in Hawai'i, researchers have been collecting photos of oceanic whitetips to start understanding local population dynamics.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

The oceanic whitetip shark is found from surface level to at least 200 meters in depth and can be found in pelagic (open ocean) waters. Catch rates suggest that oceanic whitetips are found in shallow waters more commonly than other pelagic sharks. Little is known about the overall migrations and movements of these species, but the Hawai'i Community Tagging Program is working to tag oceanic whitetips with satellite tags around the main Hawaiian Islands to get a better understanding on their movements in Hawai'i.

## THREATS:

• Fisheries interactions. Injury and mortality can be caused by the accidental hooking • and/or entanglement of oceanic whitetips in fishing gear. Oceanic whitetips are known to steal fish like ahi and mahi mahi off of trolling lines, which has occasionally resulted in intentional shooting of the sharks by fishers. 

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

Oceanic (giant) manta rays (Mobula birostris) and reef manta rays (Manta alfredi) are two species are often confused, but in 2011 the genetic difference between species confirmed the visual differences that were observed. The oceanic manta is the world's largest ray, with a wingspan ranging from 6 to 22 feet across and weighing up to 5,300 pounds. The reef manta is smaller, ranging from 4 to 12 feet across. Both kinds of manta ray are often solitary most of their lives, but aggregate around food resources, cleaning stations, or in mating trains. Manta rays are planktonic filter feeders. They each have a spot pattern on their ventral (under) side that makes each one unique, allowing them to be monitored over time using photo identification. Manta rays can live over 45 years, based on photo-identification records. Reef manta rays gestation is 12-13 months, very little is known of oceanic manta ray life history. They have among the lowest fecundity of all elasmobranchs, typically giving birth to a single pup every couple years.

## DISTRIBUTION:

The oceanic manta is a pelagic species, meaning they spend most of their time in deep water, but are occasionally seen coming close to shore. The reef manta ray is more often found in shallower waters.

## ABUNDANCE:

In 2018, the oceanic manta ray was listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Globally, their populations have declined, primarily due to bycatch in commercial fisheries combined with the international rise in demand for gill rakers. Due to its pelagic nature, the oceanic manta ray can be difficult to study, so there is still much to learn about their ecology and home range. Currently the reef manta ray is not listed under the Endangered Species Act, but they are listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Species Status: IUCN Red List: Not considered Endemic: Yes

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

The Spiny Lobster family (Palinuridae) is characterized by lobsters that lack enlarged claws, which distinguishes them from true lobsters. These species are well-protected by sharp, forward-pointing spines along their exoskeleton. Spiny lobsters, unlike other types of lobsters, do not have large claws and are generally larger-bodied. They are nocturnal feeders, often found in dark crevices or hiding under ledges in coral reefs or rocky habitats. These lobsters are highly valued in commercial and recreational fisheries, but many species, especially large individuals, are becoming increasingly rare due to heavy fishing pressure and disregard for local fishing laws. There are two key species of spiny lobsters found in Hawai'i: Ula poni (Panulirus marginatus) and Ula (Panulirus penicillatus). Both species face threats from overfishing, habitat loss, and pollution, but regulations have been put in place to protect them, including a minimum carapace length of 3.25 inches and seasonal bans on harvesting, particularly to protect breeding females.
Ula poni, or the Hawaiian Spiny Lobster, is nocturnal and carnivorous, feeding on mollusks, crustaceans, fish, and echinoderms. They spawn up to four times a year, with a female capable of producing up to half a million orange eggs each time. The eggs hatch in about four weeks, and the larvae go through several pelagic stages, lasting almost a year before returning to the reef. Juveniles are typically about one inch long. These lobsters are also known for their ability to hide in crevices, caves, or under ledges during the day. They often live near sandy areas next to healthy coral reefs, which provide both shelter and food.
Ula, or the Tufted or Green Spiny Lobster, is a large species that inhabits shallow reefs exposed to surge, often at depths of 20-60 feet. They feed on mollusks, crustaceans, and small fish. They are primarily nocturnal and can be found in rocky crevices or under ledges during the day. This species is highly valued in fisheries, but like Ula poni, it faces pressures from overfishing.
DISTRIBUTION: Ula poni are historically found throughout the Hawaiian Islands, still present across the archipelago today. However, their distribution and abundance have been significantly impacted by overfishing. The larvae typically move with ocean currents, traveling northwest along the archipelago's ridge and then southeast and southwest. The pelagic distribution of larvae is still an area of ongoing research. Found in Hawai'i, the Indo-Pacific, and the Tropical Eastern Pacific, Ula is more common than Ula poni in some areas, including Maui and Midway Atoll. Its distribution spans the Hawaiian Islands, where it is commonly found in healthy coral reef ecosystems.

## ABUNDANCE:

Overfishing has caused a significant decline in populations. Commercial catch has been in long-term decline, with recent annual catches falling below 4,500 kilograms. The recreational catch remains unknown, though it is also suspected to be unsustainable. Although more common than Ula poni, Ula still faces threats from overfishing and habitat destruction. Its populations are more stable, but commercial and recreational harvesting still presents risks to its long-term sustainability.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

These lobsters are found in a range of depths and areas, from shallow reefs to deeper waters, with their main habitat being in crevices and caves. Healthy coral reefs are vital to their habitat. Ula prefer shallow reefs and rocky areas at depths ranging from 20 to 60 feet. Healthy coral reefs are essential for their habitat, providing both shelter and abundant food sources. THREATS: Historically, Ula poni was overharvested, especially from the 1970s to the 1990s in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. While fishing closures and regulations have been put in place, overfishing, collection for the aquarium trade, and habitat degradation still pose threats. Coral reef destruction, due to pollution and climate change, further impacts their populations. Like Ula poni, Ula is threatened by overfishing, particularly from the aquarium trade and commercial fisheries. Coral reef degradation and climate change further impact their populations by destroying their habitats and food sources.

## Marine Invertebrates

## Pūpū mo'o or chitons

## Green Chiton

Acanthochiton viridis
• Habitat: The Green Chiton is typically found on rocky substrates in the intertidal zone, especially in small depressions on limestone reef flats and under rubble in tidepools. They prefer areas with some protection from the strongest waves, such as crevices and overhangs, where they can hide during the day and emerge at night to feed. This species can also be found in shallow waters along exposed shorelines, where they adhere firmly to the rocks. • Size: The Green Chiton can grow up to 1 inch (28 millimeters) in length. It has a rounded, slightly elevated shell that extends along the body in a smooth, oblong shape. • Appearance: The shell of the Green Chiton is predominantly a light green color, but it has a characteristic pale or whitish midline. The valves are smooth at the center, with minutely granulose sides, which provide some texture and protection. The dorsum (top surface) has semi-lunar plates that extend from the sides and terminate with smooth, rounded edges. The posterior terminal valve is distinctly elongated, extending laterally with truncated edges. The anterior valve wraps evenly around the front and sides of the body. These chitons are equipped with a dense, short spiculecovered ligamental border that is dark green and vitreous, which provides additional protection. 

## Flat Chiton

Stenoplax petaloides 

## SPECIES STATUS: IUCN Red List -Not considered Endemic

## SPECIES INFOMRATION:

Chitons, also known as Pūpū mo'o in Hawaiian, are fascinating mollusks that graze on algae and serve a critical role in maintaining the health of marine ecosystems. The Green Chiton (Acanthochiton viridis) and Flat Chiton (Stenoplax petaloides) are both found in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zones of Hawai'i, thriving in environments with rocky surfaces, tidepools, and reef flats. Unlike some other mollusks, chitons have a tough exterior and are well adapted to cling to hard surfaces, even during harsh wave conditions.
Both the Green Chiton (Acanthochiton viridis) and the Flat Chiton (Stenoplax petaloides) are nocturnal grazers, primarily feeding on algae that grow on rocks in their habitat. They use their radula (a specialized feeding organ) to scrape algae and detritus off the rocks. The Green Chiton, in particular, is known for its preference for areas that provide both shelter and access to abundant food sources, including small depressions and caves within the reef structure. Chitons play a key role in controlling algal growth, preventing algae from outcompeting other species, and maintaining the balance of the ecosystem. Both species are dioecious (separate sexes), and fertilization occurs externally. During the reproductive season, the chitons release their eggs and sperm into the water column, where fertilization takes place. The embryos develop into free-swimming larvae that eventually settle on rocky surfaces, where they mature into adult chitons.

## DISTRIBUTION:

The Green Chiton (Acanthochiton viridis) is distributed primarily on the Hawaiian Islands, where it inhabits rocky reef flats and tidepools. The Flat Chiton (Stenoplax petaloides) also has a similar range, being found throughout Hawai'i, particularly in shallow waters and reef flats. While both species are common within their range, habitat destruction and ocean acidification may pose future risks to their populations.

## ABUNDANCE:

The abundance of chitons is not well studied, but they are considered locally abundant in suitable habitats, especially in areas where rocky reefs and tidepools are healthy and intact. However, like many marine species, chitons are likely affected by human activities such as coastal development, pollution, and over-harvesting of algae.
LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT: Key habitats for both species are in rocky and hard substrates found in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zones. These habitats are essential for providing the food sources and shelter necessary for chiton survival. Healthy reef flats and tidepools, along with natural rock outcroppings, are critical for maintaining stable chiton populations.

## THREATS:

Both species face threats from habitat destruction caused by coastal development, pollution, and the effects of climate change, including ocean acidification and coral reef degradation. While they are not targeted specifically by fisheries, their habitats are vulnerable to human impacts, which could lead to declines in population. Climate change may also alter the composition of algae in their habitats, potentially affecting their food sources.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

Efforts to conserve chitons primarily focus on maintaining and restoring healthy reef habitats. Protecting the natural intertidal and subtidal zones from development and pollution is essential for the long-term survival of these species. Additionally, conservation strategies can include public education about the importance of protecting marine ecosystems and reducing human impacts on reef habitats.

## MONITORING:

Ongoing monitoring of chiton populations and the health of their habitats is necessary to assess the effectiveness of conservation efforts. Regular surveys in known habitats will help track population trends and the impact of environmental stressors, such as pollution and climate change.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

• Larval Distribution: Further study is needed to understand the distribution of chiton larvae, including how ocean currents affect their movement and settlement patterns. 

## Hawaiian oyster

Dendostrea sandvicensis
• Habitat: The Hawaiian oyster is commonly found on hard reefs in shallow waters, typically in quiet bays and harbors. These oysters thrive in environments with minimal water movement, where they can attach to rocky substrates and enjoy the protection of their surroundings. 

## SPECIES STATUS: IUCN Red List -Not considered Endemic SPECIES INFORMATION:

The Hawaiian oyster (Dendostrea sandvicensis) is a relatively understudied bivalve that is native to Hawai'i. It primarily inhabits shallow marine environments, attaching to hard surfaces such as rocks and reef structures. While much of its life history remains unknown, this oyster plays a significant role in the local marine ecosystem by filtering water and contributing to the overall health of the coral reef system. Its strong attachment to hard surfaces makes it an important species for reef stability and biodiversity.

## DISTRIBUTION:

The exact distribution of the Hawaiian oyster is not well-documented, but it is generally found in shallow waters around the Hawaiian Islands. Its populations are likely scattered across hard reefs in bays and harbors, though further surveys are needed to better understand its range.

## ABUNDANCE:

The abundance of this species is currently unknown. Due to limited research, it is unclear whether populations are stable, declining, or facing pressures from human activity. More studies are needed to establish population trends and determine conservation priorities.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

The Hawaiian oyster is found in sheltered areas with stable water conditions, particularly in bays and harbors. These habitats often feature coralline algae-covered rocks, which provide the oysters with attachment points. The condition of these habitats may be influenced by factors such as pollution, sedimentation, and changes in water quality, all of which can impact the health of the oyster populations. and 'opihi 'alinalina. Spawning information is sparse for the 'opihi 'ōma'o and 'opihi ko'ele, but it is believed to occur during new moon phases. 'Opihi makaiauli grow to 40 millimeters (1.6 inches) in diameter, 'opihi 'ōma'o grow to 43 millimeters (1.7 inches), the 'opihi 'alinalina grow to 32 millimeters (1.3 inches), and 'opihi ko'ele grow to 90 millimeters (3.5 inches). Once fully grown, 'opihi makaiauli is characterized by a tall round shell, 'opihi 'ōma'o is characterized by a steep sided shell, 'opihi 'alinalina is characterized by a shorter oblong shell, 'opihi ko'ele is characterized by a flat shell that is thin in juveniles and relatively disproportionately massive in large adults. Intertidal thais gastropods, predatory sea snails, are the predominant predator of 'opihi in Hawai'i. The 'opihi can evade their predators by utilising different methods of fleeing; these methods include stretching the mantle over the shell or "mantle-folding", raising the shell off the rock or "mushrooming", and extending the tentacles on the mantle. When confronted by a predatory gastropod, 'opihi makaiauli has short mantle tentacles and a long evasion distance, 'opihi 'alinalina has long mantle tentacles and a short evasion distance, and 'opihi ko'ele has mantle tentacles of varying lengths. This characteristic is unknown for 'opihi 'ōma'o. In addition to harvesting these 'opihi for consumption, native Hawaiians also used the 'opihi shells as scrapers and tools for various activities.

## DISTRIBUTION:

The primary ranges for the 'opihi makaiauli, 'opihi 'alinalina, and 'opihi ko'ele are along the basalt shorelines of the Main Hawaiian Islands; however, the 'opihi makaiauli has been found on La Perouse Pinnacle and 'opihi 'alinalina on Necker and Nihoa. The 'opihi 'ōma'o is found primarily in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, but it has been occasionally collected from Kaua'i. Historically, it was found on O'ahu and Maui as well.

## ABUNDANCE:

The abundance of 'opihi makaiauli and 'opihi 'alinalina have declined in the past decades. 'Opihi ko'ele is rare, especially so on Kaua'i and O'ahu. Abundance of 'opihi 'ōma'o is unknown. The amount of 'opihi caught and reported by commercial fisheries fluctuate from year to to year, however, in 2021 the amount of 'opihi (Cellana spp.) caught in pounds by commercial fisheries in Hawai'i reported a 3.65% increase compared with the short-term average taken from 2011 to 2020 and a 12.4% increase compared with the long-term average taken from 2001 to 2020. The recreational fishery catch is unknown.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

The primary habitat for 'opihi is the rocky intertidal zone to ten feet deep waters. 'Opihi makaiauli thrives in the spray zone or the high-shore zone, although it may be found seaward to the calcareous algal zone. It is well suited for this variable environment due to its ability to ventilate its mantle cavity when it is dry and combat the thermal stress of the environment at low tide. 'Opihi 'alinalina are found on and below the zero tide mark where there is a steady splash or the mid-shore zone, and they are often found on coralline algae. They have morphologically adapted to survive in this environment where the hydrodynamic forces are most severe. 'Opihi ko'ele are found in the low-shore zone which is below the tide mark from 0.5 to three meters (one to ten feet) deep, often between boulders. They spend the most time underwater, increasing their risk of encounters with pelagic predators. There is less known of 'opihi 'ōma'o, it is known to be found throughout the intertidal zone, but is believed to mainly inhabit the low-shore zone.

## THREATS:

• Localized heavy harvesting pressure is the most significant threat to all 'opihi species, especially 'opihi ko'ele. Populations in the wild have decreased greatly and

## Marine Invertebrates

Other Anthozoans

## Octocorals

Bicolor Grogorian

## Melithaea bicolor

The bicolor gorgonian is rare, typically found under ledges and in caverns exposed to surge. This species forms small colonies, attaining heights of approximately 3 inches (7.5 cm). Colonies are brightly colored, displaying variations of red with yellow tentacles or entirely yellow, white, or light pink. Endemic to Hawaiʻi, this species was formerly classified as Acabaria bicolor. The gorgonian's eighttentacled polyps possess an internal skeleton, which aids its survival in high-surge environments. Feeding primarily on plankton and suspended organic particles, its polyps exhibit limited stinging capabilities compared to other cnidarians.

## Blue Soft Coral

## Sarcothelia edmondsoni

This octocoral is common on vertical surfaces exposed to surge, particularly along the west coast of Hawaiʻi. It exhibits a spectrum of colors from light blue to purplish brown, depending on the density of reflective sclerites embedded in its body wall. The blue soft coral harbors symbiotic zooxanthellae, which provide it with nutrients through photosynthesis. This coral is endemic to
Hawaiʻi and was previously known as Anthelia edmondsoni. Colonies can grow up to 30 cm (12 inches) across, and its polyps reach approximately 1 cm (0.4 inches) in height.

## Molokai Leather Coral Sinularia molokaiensis

The Molokaʻi leather coral is an exceptionally rare soft coral species, with only a few known colonies globally, all recorded from Molokaʻi. It encrusts limestone or volcanic rocks in fore reef environments at depths of 1-6 meters (3-20 feet).
Colonies can attain sizes of 30 cm (12 inches) across. This species relies on plankton as its primary food source and exhibits remarkable resilience in high-energy reef systems.

## 'Ōkole or Anemones

Hawaiian Mann's Anenome Cladactella manni
Found in dark crevices and pockets within the intertidal zone, Hawaiian Mann's anemones are uncommon and brightly colored, with vivid red tentacles. These solitary anemones grow up to 10 cm (4 inches) in diameter and are endemic to Hawaiʻi. They utilize both zooxanthellae symbiosis and planktonic feeding for nutrition. Reproduction occurs both sexually, with the release of gametes, and asexually through tissue fragmentation, primarily from the foot.

## Sand Anenome

## Heteractis malu

The sand anemone is rare and occurs in sandy rubble habitats at various depths. Although formerly abundant in Kāneʻohe Bay and Māʻalaea Bay, its populations have significantly declined. Specimens are white with intricate fluorescence patterns in orange, green, blue, or violet, often accented with purple-tipped tentacles. These anemones may harbor commensal organisms such as shrimp (Thor amboinensis) or juvenile Hawaiian dascyllus. They can reach up to 12 inches (30 cm) in diameter but are usually much smaller. This species is distributed across Hawaiʻi, the East Indian Ocean, and the tropical Pacific.

## Zoanthids

## White Stripe Zoanthid Palythoa mutuki

Locally common in shallow waters, this species attaches to rubble or rock, particularly in bays. Its polyps, measuring up to 3 cm (1.2 inches) tall, are spaced apart and exhibit a striking green disc with bold white radial stripes and white knobs between long tentacles. The body wall incorporates sand, lending rigidity. Contact should be avoided, as it contains potentially deadly palytoxins. Its distribution spans from the Persian Gulf to Hawaiʻi.

## Sunray Zoanthid

## Palythoa heliodiscus

Occasionally observed on shaded vertical surfaces in shallow, wave-exposed areas, the sunray zoanthid has loosely spaced polyps with short, stubby tentacles. Its coloration includes tan polyps with brown discs marked by fine radial lines.
Polyps grow to a diameter of 1 inch (2.5 cm). Like other zoanthids, it may produce palytoxins, requiring caution during handling. This species is distributed from Okinawa and Queensland to Hawaiʻi.

## Rubbery or Pillow Zoanthids

## Palythoa tuberculosa

This species commonly forms extensive mats in areas subjected to wave surge. Polyps often remain closed under rough conditions. The texture of the colony resembles hard rubber, and coloration ranges from white to gray or brown. Palytoxins are present, necessitating careful handling. Its range includes Hawaiʻi and the Indo-Pacific. Formerly known as Palythoa caesia.

## Kealakekua Zoanthid

## Zoanthus kealakekuaensis

Endemic to Hawaiʻi, this zoanthid is locally common along basalt ledges near the waterline. Its tightly packed, fluorescent green polyps form mats.
Each polyp measures approximately 5 mm (0.

A common hermit crab found in shallow waters exposed to wave action. It attains a size of about 3/4 inch and is more aggressive than other species in the Calcinus genus. Its striking red-and-blue coloration makes it easily recognizable. Endemic to Hawai'i, it was previously misidentified as the Indo-Pacific species Calcinus elegans.

## Lsurent's Hermit Crab Calcinus laurentae

This species is common in branching coral deeper than 20 feet. Distinguished by its white claws with black joints, red walking legs with black-andwhite tips, and unique black eyes dotted with white. Reaching only 1/4 inch, it is one of the smaller hermit crabs endemic to Hawai'i. Prefers deeper coral reef habitats.

## Cinetorhynchus hawaiiensis

A small shrimp endemic to Hawai'i, commonly seen in finger corals at night. Notable for its dark spot on the side of the abdomen. Reaches up to 1 inch in length and contributes to reef health by foraging for organic matter.

## Henderson's Hinge-Beak Shrimp Cinetorhynchus hendersoni

Common in coral-rich areas at night, this shrimp exhibits gray coloration with red-orange reticulations, and juveniles may appear bluegreen. Reaches up to 3 inches in length and ranges across Hawai'i and the Indo-Pacific. No previous scientific name recorded.

A nocturnal species, this shrimp is recognized for the knotted, bulbous bumps on its body. It resides in crevices or under rocks during the day, feeding on plankton and detritus. Rathbun's Hinge-Beaked Shrimp Rhynchocinetes rathbunae
A colorful and slender species, Rathbun's shrimp is easily recognized by its distinctive hinge-shaped beak. It is typically found in coral and rock crevices, where it feeds on small organisms. Endemic to Hawai'i and the Indo-Pacific, it plays an important role in the balance of reef ecosystems.

Known for its vivid red and white coloration, this shrimp has prominent antennae and often occurs in pairs. It feeds on detritus, contributing to the health of coral reef ecosystems. Endemic to Hawai'i, it is a striking and important member of the reef community.

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

All stony corals feed on small plankton or dissolved organic matter that is in the waters. Most corals use nematocysts on their tentacles to capture and sting prey, feeding primarily at night. Other species, such as Pavona duerdeni, are suspension feeders. Stony corals with endosymbiotic dinoflagellates can get up to 98 percent of their nutrition from the sugars produced by the algae. Balanophyllia and Tubastraea lack endosymbiotic dinoflagellates,. Stony corals reproduce both sexually and asexually. For sexually reproducing species, a particular combination of day length, tide, and moonlight prompts spawning events. Corals can also reproduce asexually, through planulation, budding, or fragmentation. orals such as the Pocillopora sp. and Porites sp. brood their eggs and release the larvae or planulae completely formed. Budding is when a coral polyp divides into a genetically identical new polyp while maintaining tissue connections with the colony, while fragmentationis when pieces are broken off and grow into new colonies. ## Marine Limu

SPECIES STATUS: This fact sheet is inclusive to all the native and endemic limu species listed in Appendix B.

## SPECIES INFORMATION

Marine algae, or limu, are categorized into three main groups: brown algae (Phaeophyceae), green algae (Chlorophyta), and red algae (Rhodophyta). While all groups contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis, their distinctive colors come from other pigments. Limu play several vital roles in coral reef ecosystems. These roles include stabilizing the reef, cycling nutrients, supporting primary productivity (photosynthesis that produces oxygen), generating sand, and serving as a key food source for many marine species.
Crustose coralline algae (CCA) are tough algae that incorporate calcium carbonate into their cell walls. They play a crucial role in holding the reef together and protecting its structure from erosion and damage, promoting both reef stability and growth. CCA also stimulate coral larvae to settle by releasing chemical signals, providing an ideal surface for corals to attach and grow.
Halimeda kanaloana, a green algae species composed of calcified segments, thrives in sandy environments and forms extensive meadows at depths of up to 260 feet. After dying, its calcified remains significantly contribute to the sand and sediment composition of coral reefs. Limu pālahalaha (Ulva fasciata), or sea lettuce, is another green algae species that helps prevent erosion, produces oxygen, creates sand, and serves as a vital food source for marine animals, forming the foundation of the food chain in local fisheries.
Limu also have deep cultural and historical significance in Hawaiian society, playing a major role in the traditional diet and serving various medicinal, religious, and cultural purposes. While men typically fished offshore in canoes, women gathered food from the nearshore environment, women were the primary gatherers and experts in limu. Due to kapu (sacred restrictions) that limited their diet, women became specialists in limu, collecting and preparing it for the community, because limu was considered noa (free of restriction).
limu pālahalaha and limu kohu (Asparagopsis taxiformis) hold significant roles in traditional diets, rituals, and practices. Limu pālahalaha is a staple food often consumed with fish or poi, valued for its mild flavor and high nutritional content. It also carries symbolic importance in representing sustainability and the connection between land and sea. Limu pālahalaha was used to make leis and other ornamentations for hula dancers. Limu kohu, a prized delicacy, is cherished for its strong, spicy flavor and reddish color. It was traditionally served during special occasions and feasts. Both limu types have spiritual and medicinal roles, with limu kohu believed to have healing properties and both limu representing abundance, balance, and prosperity in Hawaiian culture.
Sargassum echinocarpum, or limu kala, is a brown algae species that was designated as the official state limu in 2023 and holds significant cultural importance. It is traditionally used in ho'oponopono, or forgiveness ceremonies, where participants receive a piece of limu kala, offer prayers, and consume it at the ceremony's conclusion. Additionally, kahu (priests) used it for cleansing rituals, mixing it with turmeric and salt water to purify individuals, objects, or places. Limu kala is also linked to 'opelu, playing a role in rituals performed by fishers at the start of the 'opelu fishing season. Additionally, this species grows in free floating mats which provides microhabitats, protection, and breeding ground for many marine species.

## DISTRIBUTION:

All species are native or endemic to the Main Hawaiian Islands. Polysiphonia rubrorhiza, is a limu species that is endemic to the North Western Hawaiian Islands.

## ABUNDANCE:

Hawai'i's endemic marine algae include red algae (16.7%), green algae (6.6%), and brown algae (2.8%), which totals 26.1% of the total marine flora in Hawai'i. Many native limu species, such as limu kohu and limu pālahalaha, are not as abundant as they once were and have declined due to urban development, unsustainable harvesting, non-native species, climate change, and the decline of traditional knowledge and practices.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Red algae, the most diverse and abundant in Hawai'i, thrive in habitats from shallow waters to deep depths, up to 100 meters, due to their ability to absorb blue light. Green algae prefer shallow, well-lit environments like tide pools and rocky shores, requiring high light levels for photosynthesis. Brown algae, less common in Hawai'i, inhabit cooler waters and rocky coastlines at intermediate depths with moderate wave action.

## THREATS:

• Habitat loss via changing coastlines with shoreline development, bloom-forming algae encroaching on shoreline habitat and climate change. • Alien and invasive species.
• Land-derived pollutants.
• Anthropogenic induced reductions in surface and groundwater flow to the nearshore environment.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

Actions include the continuation of the following:
• Protecting and restoring key marine habitats, including coral reefs and tide pools.
• Conducting outreach and education of the cultural and ecological importance of marine limu. • Continuing to control, manage, and prevent introduced alien and invasive algae.
• Repopulating native species.

## CHAPTER 8: IMPLEMENTATION, MONITORING, AND ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT IMPLEMENTATION OF HAWAI'I'S SWAP

Global biodiversity is being lost at an unprecedented rate in human history, threatening ecosystem services, national economies, food security, and the well-being of societies. Island ecosystems are particularly vulnerable, and native ecosystems of the Hawaiian Islands are no exception. Over 60% of habitats have been destroyed or severely degraded, leading to the extinction of hundreds of species, with hundreds more at risk.
More than 6,000 species are identified in this Hawaii State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) as Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and more than 500 hundred species are endangered or at risk of extinction. The threats facing these species, detailed in Chapter 4 of the SWAP, are numerous and widespread, affecting virtually every SGCN and native ecosystem type.
The conservation lands identified in Chapter 6 for targeted conservation actions encompass over two million acres of public and private lands across the archipelago, including remote and rugged terrain. The extensive number of species, the range of interrelated threats, and scale and complexity of conservation lands pose significant logistical and financial challenges for effectively managing threats to biodiversity.
The effectiveness of conservation management varies depending on the biology and status of the species, the type and number of threats, the condition of the habitat, and the scale at which conservation actions are implemented. Some threats, such as ungulate control and fencing, can be addressed at relatively large spatial scales covering thousands of acres. Others, however, such as mammalian predators and invertebrate pests, can typically only be managed at small spatial scales, leading to exceedingly high per-unit costs. Still others are interrelated, requiring that management be done concurrently or sequentially. For most species, controlling a wide range of threats at multiple spatial scales is essential for preventing species extinction and achieving recovery goals.
Given current funding limitations, it is not currently feasible to manage all threats across all areas where SGCN exist. Therefore, conservation efforts must be guided by a strategic approach that optimizes cost-effective actions in essential habitats. Effective planning is critical to ensuring the protection and recovery of species and the ecosystems on which they depend. However, even the best plans can be difficult to implement when dealing with hundreds of at-risk species spanning plants, invertebrates, and vertebrates. Conservation planning is further complicated by novel threats, the accelerating effects of climate change, and limited financial resources. Thus, a conservation approach needs to include clear guidance for effective implementation.

## The Maui Nui Landscape Conservation Plan

To address these challenges, the Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources, in collaboration with a broad coalition of public and private agencies, organizations, landowners, and conservation experts, is developing an innovative approach to implementation planning for biodiversity conservation in Hawaii. Initially focused on Maui Nui, the Maui Nui Landscape Conservation Plan (MNLCP) provides a systematic, climate-resilient approach to landscape-scale conservation. It integrates species-specific recovery goals into spatially explicit, multi-species conservation areas while optimizing cost-effective actions to enhance biodiversity at both population and ecosystem scales.

• Predator control for O'ahu 'elepaio (Chasiempis sandwichensis ibidis) and seabirds on O'ahu; and • Monitoring and control of remnant axis deer (Axis axis).
3) Develop and implement programs to obtain, manage, and disseminate information needed to guide conservation management and recovery programs:

Kaua'i, O'ahu, and Hawai'i;
 • Surveys for nest colony locations of 'ua'u and 'a'o;
• Research on Blackburn's sphinx moth populations; and • Survey and monitoring of population status of, threats to, and the success of predator control efforts to protect native terrestrial snails on O'ahu.
In addition, other sources of state and federal funding are being used to address all seven objectives in the next fiscal year. For example, the DLNR general fund budget supports management of existing NARs and watershed management projects, and the State Legislature included a line-item of 4 million dollars in the state budget for each of Fiscal Years 2015 and 2016 to address invasive species issues. Federal funds through grant programs administered by USFWS, NOAA, and U.S. Forest Service are used to protect habitat and control invasive species. A variety of funding sources are used to support research and outreach efforts. The successful partnerships and collaboration on SWAP projects will continue.

## ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT AND THE TEN-YEAR REVISION

Evaluation of Hawai'i's SWAP is linked to practicing adaptive management. Adaptive management results in effective monitoring and evaluation of the Strategy because it allows for structured learning by doing and altering strategies in response to changing circumstances (e.g., political, environmental, economic, etc.) to ensure success in achieving conservation objectives. It is also important to recognize that there are barriers to implementation that must be accounted for as part of adaptive management. Institutional barriers include the slow nature of changing policy and regulations, difficulties in getting conservation tools approved in a timely manner, and special interests preventing implementation of needed conservation actions.
As a part of the adaptive management process, the State DOFAW and DAR will conduct annual reviews to assess Hawai'i's SWAP program implementation and determine if any changes need to be made. This review will include identification of new or altered threats; review of recent surveys, data, and research; evaluation of the effectiveness of conservation actions; identification of urgent conservation actions needed for other taxa; and consideration of issues that are preventing implementation of the SWAP. This annual review will also include the annual process of determining priorities for using SWG funding. Because Hawai'i's list of SGCNs is broad and generally covers all native taxa, consideration of potential additions or removals to the list would be done during major reviews conducted at ten-year intervals (see below), unless the annual review process identified an imminent need. Review of progress and planning for implementation of conservation projects also occurs at partner-organization meetings. The island -based watershed
Hawaiʻi's State Wildlife Action Plan October 1, 2025 partnerships, invasive species committees, and statewide coordinating groups such as the Hawai'i Invasive Species Council, Coordinating Group on Alien Pests, and Papahānaumokuākea Monument Management Board hold annual or more frequent meetings that discuss conservation project implementation, issues, and needs. DOFAW and DAR are members of these organizations and obtain valuable input through these collaborations. The SWAP website and partner contact database are additional tools that will be used to update and continue the engagement of partners in implementing, monitoring, and evaluating Hawai'i's SWAP.
Part of measuring the success of, and adaptively managing, Hawai'i's SWAP is represented by the formal ten-year revision. Each ten-year review and revision will be initiated by DLNR and will involve many of the same steps as were performed for this 2015 plan update, including comprehensively reviewing management plans and research, working closely with partners, and engaging the public to identify and incorporate new information. Ongoing monitoring and the annual reviews by DOFAW and DAR also will assist in identifying necessary revisions. The major ten-year revision should start in 2024, at least 18 months before deadline, beginning with an internal review and continuing with an outreach effort and solicitation of input from agencies, conservation partners, technical experts, and the public during the course of the 18 month review. This review will consist of analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of the SWAP, identifying barriers that prevented successful implementation, updating species and habitat information, assessing and updating the primary threats, evaluating the continued viability of the identified conservation objectives and strategies, and conducting outreach for ideas and input from partners, interested parties and public. To solicit public input on the revision, a series of public scoping meetings will be held on each island early in the 18-month process, to get the word out that the plan is being updated, and give stakeholders, conservation partners, agencies and the public ample time to review, participate in the process and provide input. The draft plan will be posted on the website and made available for public review for 60 days. The 2025 ten-year revision will provide the opportunity for continued adaptive management to ensure preservation of Hawai'i's SGCNs and native habitats and to expand the vision of malama 'āina (protecting the land) for future generations.

## MONITORING

The need for monitoring is a consistent theme throughout Hawai'i's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) and is referenced in several previous chapters 
(Chapters 4,
5,
6,
and 7)
. Chapter 8 addresses monitoring specifically in the following ways: it provides a summary of current monitoring efforts at both the taxa and habitat levels; it outlines monitoring needs and recommendations; and it discusses the implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of statewide conservation objectives as defined in Chapter 4. It also outlines processes for the next ten-year revision of the SWAP. In doing so, this chapter addresses required elements 5, 6, and 7.

## PURPOSE AND VALUE OF MONITORING

A well planned and executed monitoring program is key to the success of conservation efforts, especially in light of the scarcity of personnel and funds needed to protect and recover native wildlife resources in Hawai'i. Monitoring programs are essential to guide plans and implement adaptive changes to those plans, and for management and recovery programs to be most costeffective and achieve their goals. Monitoring does this by providing ways to track population trends, to assess threats and limiting factors, and to evaluate progress of actions to improve native wildlife status. Monitoring programs are also tools with which to communicate conservation achievements, helping to develop support for conservation actions with decision-Pacific Fisheries Information Network, the Coral Reef Information Service, and the U.S. Geological Service's (USGS's) Hawai'i Forest Bird Interagency Database Project, which analyzes information collected during yearly forest bird surveys to determine conservation needs of these species.
The challenges facing implementation of effective monitoring are similar to those challenges faced in implementing conservation actions as discussed in Chapter 4: inadequate funds, lack of trained personnel to carry out monitoring, requirements for advanced technical expertise for identification of many invertebrate taxa, insufficient tools for monitoring (e.g., practical or standardized monitoring protocols and equipment), inability to use the information collected (e.g., survey forms or collected data are never entered into a database for later data analysis), and gaps in information sharing. The biggest challenges are to design precise and efficient monitoring programs to best measure the outcomes of conservation actions and progress toward recovery goal and to have adaptive management respected and funded at a level commensurate with it's importance to conservation. For example, while monitoring relatively populous species can be fairly straightforward, the cost and difficulty of monitoring rare or highly fluctuating populations presents difficult trade-offs between money applied toward gaining precise knowledge of population status and money needed for species and habitat improvement or restoration.

## TAXON MONITORING

Most monitoring in the state consists of counting individuals and reproductive success. For many taxa, appropriate monitoring programs are specified in recovery or management plans.
The level of detail of management recommendations provided in the plans varies among taxa.
The following outlines existing monitoring efforts and resources for taxa as well as identifies gaps and needs.

## Terrestrial Mammal

The 'ōpe'ape'a (Lasiurus cinereus semotus [Hawaiian hoary bat]) is the only land mammal native to the Hawaiian archipelago. The USFWS recovery plan for the bat was developed in 1998 and outlines the monitoring requirements for this species. Specific recommendations center on the need for island-wide surveys and monitoring to determine bat population levels and distribution, as well as associated key habitats and potential threats affecting populations. USGS has been conducting systematic acoustic monitoring on Hawai'i for five years and collected bat occupancy data at study sites by season and across annual cycles. Acoustic monitoring with similar goals is underway on Maui, Kaua'i, and O'ahu, with the intent to obtain data on seasonal and annual patterns of bat habitat use. The wide range of habitat and the limited technology available to detect bat presence makes monitoring this species difficult. USGS is currently coordinating Hawaiian bat research efforts with USFWS, the Division of Forestry and Wildlife (DOFAW), the U.S. Department of Defense, the National Park Service (NPS), private landowners, and the forest products industry to improve monitoring of this species.

## Forest Birds

Hawai'i's native forest birds are perhaps the best monitored species in the state. However, monitoring efforts for even these species could be improved, particularly life history monitoring for specific species. plans identifying monitoring needs for identified critical species. Elements of monitoring from these plans are conducted by USFWS, DOFAW, and their partners; however, the full range of monitoring recommendations has yet to be implemented. Refinement of species-specific survey protocols is needed to provide managers with the best possible information, such as how best to survey the Maui parrotbill (Pseudonestor xanthophrys).
For non-endangered forest birds such as 'i'iwi (Vestiaria coccinea), 'apapane (Himatione sanguinea), and 'amakihi (Hemignathus virens), monitoring occurs during the forest bird surveys and during monitoring conducted on managed lands. Significant monitoring can be focused on assessing the trend status of birds targeted for listing (i.e., the i'iwi). For the more common birds, their potential dispersal in lower elevations may require different monitoring protocols. There are no wild populations of 'alalā (Corvus hawaiiensis [Hawaiian crow])-all existing populations are in captive propagation facilities, which are closely monitored by staff.
Monitoring protocols for the release of 'alalā into the wild have been developed and will be used for planned releases in 2016.

## Raptors

There is no systematic island-wide monitoring for pueo (Asio flammeus sandwichensis [Hawaiian short-eared owl]). Population assessments are based on surveys conducted on an opportunistic or piece-meal basis, such as research surveys by graduate students, surveys of species on various managed lands, and Hawai'i Audubon counts. USFWS conducted intensive monitoring for 'io (Buteo solitarius [Hawaiian hawk]) during 2007 and found that the population has been stable for at least 20 years and occupies 59 percent of the island. USFWS proposed that the 'io be delisted and has developed a post-delisting monitoring plan for the species. That plan will involve island-wide variable circular-plot surveys, employing playback recordings, and conducted every five years if implemented.

## Waterbirds

All endemic Hawaiian waterbirds are the subject of USFWS recovery plans that outline monitoring needs and actions. A draft recovery plan and conservation action plan for the nēnē (Branta sandvicensis [Hawaiian goose]) 
(USFWS 2004
(USFWS , 2012) )
 Although the twice-annual waterbird count conducted by DOFAW is considered the best tool available for estimating relative abundance of waterbirds, it could be improved with greater standardization and consistency among islands. Areas that need attention include identification of koloa maoli, mallards, and hybrids; greater consistency in coverage of wetlands each year; development of more accurate methods of surveying 'alae 'ula (such as using playbacks); and coverage of montane stream habitats to better detect koloa maoli populations.
Seabirds 
October 1, 2025
 The majority of Hawai'i's seabird populations are in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.
Monitoring of these species is conducted by USFWS at Midway, Laysan, and French Frigate Shoals and by DOFAW at Kure Atoll. Extensive work is being done to control and eradicate invasive weeds and increase monitoring capacity at Kure. Banding and monitoring of seabirds is an element of the natural resources science plan for Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument.
In the Main Hawaiian Islands, seabirds nest mostly on offshore islands and islets. Monitoring of these populations is conducted on some islands by DOFAW as well as by an interagency organization. Seabirds also are monitored in known nesting areas on managed lands, and through DOFAW's twice-annual statewide waterbird surveys. 

## Northwestern Hawaiian Islands Passerines and Waterbird

Given the small population levels and restricted range of these species, monitoring is intensively conducted by USFWS through the NWR system, and on Kure Atoll by DOFAW. Monitoring programs were developed and implemented in association with translocation programs for Laysan duck (Anas laysanensis) and the Nihoa millerbird (Acrocephalus familiaris kingi). The USFWS Revised Recovery Plan for the Laysan Duck (2009) identifies the monitoring protocol.
Monitoring in association with the translocations is ongoing.

## Terrestrial Invertebrates

In contrast to the limited, but relatively consistent monitoring of terrestrial vertebrates, terrestrial invertebrate populations are not adequately monitored. Limited baseline densities have been obtained for some taxa in a few locations. USFWS draft recovery plans discuss the monitoring needs of O'ahu tree snails (Achatinella spp.), Blackburn's sphinx moth, and the Kaua'i cave arthropods (Adelocosa anops and Spelaeorchestia koloana). The challenge of adequately monitoring terrestrial invertebrates lies in the sheer number of species (over 5,000) that exist in Hawai'i, the fact that these species are quite small (averaging less than 5 millimeters in size), and the limited number of people who are trained to identify these species.

## Plants and Algae

Systematic monitoring of rare plant populations occurs in selected management areas such as Forest Reserves, NARs, National Parks, NWRs, TNC preserves, and other protected areas. No systematic statewide monitoring occurs for these species. Various land managers individually monitor the status of the plants on their lands. In highly managed areas, the existence and condition of rare plants may be well known (e.g., if rare plants are identified within fenced enclosures in an NAR or Forest Reserve or within Special Ecological Units in a National Park).
For more remote or less actively managed areas under protection (e.g., many Forest Reserves), historical surveys may indicate the previous existence of rare plants, but information on their current status is limited. Finally, information regarding rare plant distribution or abundance is not always shared with the Hawai'i Biodiversity and Mapping Program and may remain solely within the control of a landowner or land management agency. Plants and Their Ecosystems. This draft plan recognizes the importance of monitoring to rare plant conservation and identifies areas needing further field surveys to determine the current status of rare plants, totaling approximately 13 percent of the state (202,000 hectares or 500,000 acres). Marine algae are systematically monitored in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Other marine plants or freshwater algae would be surveyed in association with preparation of an environmental assessment or other requirement for project development.

## Freshwater Species

The State Division of Aquatic Resources (DAR), Department of Land and Natural Resources (DLNR) Water Commission, NPS, and the University of Hawai'i conducted comprehensive surveys of 376 perennial streams across Hawai'i for the 
Hawai'i Stream Assessment Project (Commission on Water Resources Management 1990)
. The assessment collected data on presence of native species and evaluated the stream for developed a database on stream condition that is maintain and used today for monitoring stream conditions. In its monitoring program, DAR collects information on native and non-native species of fish, crustaceans, mollusks, insects, and algae and enters it into the database. Stream assessments are done on an individual project basis to evaluate impacts of project developments and do not occur statewide on a regular basis. DAR continues to maintain the stream assessment database. These data are used in monitoring, assessing, managing, and protecting the freshwater aquatic resources of the state. Techniques used include point quadrat count method, drift sampling, larval trapping, and other scientific surveys (insects, algae) by other institutions or organizations. There is no systematic statewide survey of freshwater species.

## Anchialine Pond Fauna

Hawai'i has a large number of anchialine ponds, but very few (such as at ʻĀhihi-Kīnaʻu, Maui, and Lua o Palahemo, Hawaiʻi) have been systematically surveyed. Threats to anchialine pool ecosystems include changes in water quality and quantity because of groundwater withdrawal, accidental and deliberate introduction of non-indigenous species including alien plants, fish, arthropods, and molluscs, and historical loss of pool complexes following coastal resort development. USFWS and NPS have identified anchialine pools as priority ecosystems in need of research to better understand the habitat requirements of endemic pool biota and how they will respond to current and future changes in pool ecosystems. USGS is conducting surveys of anchialine pools, focusing primarily on three national parks on Hawai'i island with significant pool resources: Hawai'i Volcanoes, Kaloko-Honokōau, and Pu'uhonua o Hōaunau. Information collected includes physical and biological habitat characteristics and the relative densities of rare anchialine pool invertebrates at individual pools. Assessments of many anchialine pond fauna and habitat have occurred over the years, but no systematic monitoring takes place.

## Marine Species

Routine marine monitoring has been a component of DAR's activities for over 50 years. Early efforts concentrated on using in-water visual assessments to measure resource fish stocks and changes to those stocks within marine protected areas and at artificial reef sites. For the past 15 to 20 years, efforts have been made to improve upon research methods, increase the frequency of surveys, expand the number of areas covered by assessments, and study changes associated with new management initiatives. Current efforts are focused on annual assessments of coral reef ecosystems across a range of management areas. Surveys document the abundance of resource fish and herbivorous fish, smaller cryptic fish and recruits, urchins and larger mobile

## MONITORING NEEDS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Though Hawai'i has a foundation for monitoring of species and habitats, this foundation needs to be expanded by strengthening existing efforts and developing new ones. Specific monitoring needs are identified at the taxa level in Chapter 7 and at the habitat level in Chapters 5 and 6 in the Management Needs sections. Additionally, monitoring needs are outlined in Chapter 4 in the Threats and Statewide Objectives and Strategies sections.
This section addresses specific monitoring gaps for species groupings as well as statewide initiatives. Where new efforts are required, the approach will be to focus on relevant, realistic, and effective monitoring and evaluation that is cost-effective, sustainable, and has minimal adverse impacts on native ecosystems. The recommendations are discussed below.

## DEVELOP MONITORING WORKING GROUPS

The establishment of statewide monitoring working groups for different species, habitats, or threats will help to facilitate the development and implementation of needed monitoring actions. These working groups will provide expert advice to guide monitoring of species and habitats in the state. The working groups will help identify monitoring gaps, prioritize needs, develop strategies and recommended actions to address monitoring issues, and guide implementation of monitoring actions.

## IMPROVE MONITORING FOR ALL TAXA

The following monitoring needs, based on species groupings, are listed in order from the groups that are not systematically monitored to those needing improved monitoring efforts.
• Most invertebrate populations are neither well-characterized nor adequately monitored. Coordinated efforts are needed to develop and implement plans to increase inventory and monitoring statewide. Taxa requiring these efforts include terrestrial arthropods, land and tree snails, anchialine pond species, non-coral and non-regulated marine invertebrates, and deep water coral species. For host-specific terrestrial invertebrates, rare plant surveys are necessary. For land and tree snails, information is needed on the status and distribution of populations and occurrences of predators. • For freshwater fishes and aquatic invertebrates, systematic monitoring needs to be expanded to all important watersheds and areas. • For plants, coordination of different efforts and development of survey priorities is needed. • For anchialine pond fauna, monitoring of populations and distribution in known and likely habitats should continue as well as development of quantitative survey methods and methods to monitor associated interstitial and hypogeal habitats. • For the 'ōpe'ape'a, established methods and protocols for larger-scale monitoring of bat populations, and for detecting the presence of roosting individuals in thick vegetation, are needed. • For avian species, improvements are needed to expand the scope and frequency of monitoring, data management and analysis, and reporting (e.g., needs include demographic data for constructing population models and reproductive data for determining greatest threats to productivity).

## GLOSSARY

Ahupua'a: land division usually extending from the uplands to the sea, so called because the boundary was marked by a heap (ahu) of stones surmounted by the image of a pig (pua'a), or because the pig or other tribute was laid on the altar as a tax to the chief.
Ballast Water: water carried in ballast tanks in the hold of ships to help keep the ship stable. Water is usually discharged and taken up in port, which can facilitate the spread of invasive species.
Biological Diversity or Biodiversity: the variety of all biological life -plants, animals, fungi, and microorganism -and the ecosystems on land or in water where they live; the diversity of life on earth or in a particular location.
Biological Integrity: defined by the Environmental Protection Agency as "the ability of an aquatic ecosystem to support and maintain a balanced, adaptive community of organisms having a species composition, diversity, and functional organization comparable to that of natural habitats within a region."
Congener: belonging to the same genus.
Conspecific: belonging to the same species.
Critical Habitat: term defined in the Endangered Species Act. Critical habitat is defined as (1) the specific areas within the geographic area occupied by a species at the time it is listed, on which are found those physical or biological features (a) essential to the conservation of the species and (b) which may require special management considerations and (2) specific areas outside the geographical area occupied by the species at the time it is listed upon a determination that such areas are essential for the conservation of the species. Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act prohibits the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat with regard to actions carried out, funded, or authorized by a Federal agency.
Depredate: prey on.
Ecosystem: an ecological unit that is composed of interacting organisms in their environment.
Endemic: adjective or noun used to describe species found only within a specified region or locality and thus unique to that area.
Epiphytes: a plant growing on another plant for support or anchorage rather than for water or nutrients.
Euryhaline: adjective indicating ability to tolerate a large range of salinities. Eutrophication: water pollution caused by excessive nutrients that stimulate excessive plant growth.
Extant: alive, existing, not extinct.
Extirpate: not existing, extinct, wipe out or destroy completely.
Feral: adjective used to describe domesticated animal that has reverted to an untamed state.
Habitat: the area or type of environment where an organism or a biological population lives or occurs.
Holotype: the single specimen for which a species is named and described.
Hull Fouling: the attachment and/or colonization of ship hulls by organisms such as barnacles and mussels; can be a major vector for invasive species introduction.
Hypogeal: underground. Used to describe the underground, water-filled spaces where anchialine fauna live in addition to anchialine ponds.
Indigenous: species that occur naturally in a particular area (e.g., not introduced by humans or human activity). All endemic species are considered indigenous species; however, the term "indigenous" is sometimes used to describe native species that are not endemic or whose endemic status is unknown.
Interstitial: space between structures. Used to refer to the spaces where anchialine fauna are found in the hypogeal environment.
Introduced Species: species that do not arrive into ecosystems through natural means (e.g., air, wind, water, animals), but through human-assisted activities. The terms "alien," "non-native," or "exotic" species may also be used interchangeably with introduced species.
Invasive Species: an animal pest or weed that negatively impacts indigenous species and ecosystems.
Kūpuna: grandparent, ancestor, relative or close friend of the grandparent's generation, grandaunt, granduncle.
Lo'i: irrigated terrace, especially for taro, but also for rice: paddy.
Maui Nui: the islands of Moloka'i, Lāna'i, Maui, and Kaho'olawe.
Hawai'i's State Wildlife Action Plan 
October 1, 2015
 Native: species that occur naturally in a particular area (e.g., not introduced by humans or human activity). The term "native" is commonly used to describe both endemic and non-endemic indigenous species.
Niche: the function or role of an organism in an ecosystem or the habitat an organism occupies in the ecosystem.
Non-Point Source Pollution: water pollution that comes from many diffuse sources rather than from a specific point, such as an outfall pipe, and is often the result of human activities.
Phenology: temporal aspects of a species' biology (e.g., timing of a species' reproductive cycle).
Philopatry: the characteristic of remaining near or returning to a particular area (e.g., natal territory). Used to describe species that tend to remain in, or return to, their home area.
Phytophagous: same as herbivorous (plant eating), but often associated with insects that pierce and suck liquids from plants.
Phytoremediation: the process of cleaning up pollutants especially in water or soil using plants.

## PEPP: Plant Extinction Prevention (PEP) Program

Point Source Pollution: pollution from any discernible, confined, or discrete conveyance from which pollutants are or may be discharged, including, (but not limited to) pipes, ditches, channels, tunnels, conduits, wells, containers, rolling stock, concentrated animal feeding operations, or vessels.
Precocial: offspring that exhibit a high level of independent activity from hatching. Usually applies to birds or mammals.
Recovery Habitat: term used by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for areas identified in Recovery Plans and determined to be necessary for long-term survival and recovery of endangered species.
Shield Volcano: defined by the U.S. Geological Service to refer to volcanoes with broad, gentle slopes, built by the eruption of fluid basalt lava.
Species: a group of closely related, interbreeding organisms that produce fertile offspring.
Stochastic: unpredictable or by chance.

 Statutorily designated regulated areas are specific regions that are defined and regulated by law for the purpose of conservation, management, or other forms of oversight. These areas are managed to protect natural resources, wildlife, or cultural heritage. The designation of these areas helps maintain sustainable use, preserve ecosystems, and provide guidelines for human activities within them. ## Bottomfish Restricted Fishing Areas

Bottomfish Restricted Fishing Areas (BRFAs) are managed by DAR and were established in 1998 after encouragement by the Western Pacific Fisheries Management Council and consultation with an ad hoc committee and extensive public comment. There are 12 BRFAs. Their goal is to protect stocks of bottomfish in the Main Hawaiian Islands. No fishing for state-defined bottomfish species was allowed from 2007 -2019, after which the BLNR approved reopening of four, and in 2022, all BRFAs.

## Fish Replenishment Areas

Fish Replenishment Areas (FRAs) are managed by DAR and were established in 2000 in order to replenish and protect the stocks of marine aquarium fishes on the island of Hawai'i. The goal of FRAs is to address declining fish populations, habitat degradation and overfishing pressures, especially among commercial aquarium fishers and other resource users. No commercial or recreational aquarium fish collecting or fish feeding is allowed. There are nine FRAs in within the West Hawaiʻi Regional Fishery Managment Area.

## EXISTING REGULATIONS Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) establishes import and export restrictions and regulations to protect living and dead animals and plants and their parts from excessive extractive use and international trade.

## Migratory Bird Treaty Act

The Migratory Bird Treaty Act is the domestic law that implements the United States' commitment to four international conventions (with Canada, Japan, Mexico, and Russia)
for the protection of migratory birds. Each of the conventions protect selected species of birds that are common to the U.S. and the other country (i.e., they occur in both countries at some point during their annual life cycle).

## Federal Endangered Species Act

The ESA was passed in 1973, to prevent the extinction of species. The current purpose of the ESA is to conserve the ecosystems on which threatened and endangered species depend and to conserve and recover listed species. A species may be listed as threatened if it is likely to become endangered within the foreseeable future, and a species may be listed as endangered if it is in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range. In addition, listed species receive regulatory protection, as taking (which includes injuring or killing) a listed species is prohibited under the ESA. In addition, the ESA requires federal agencies to consult with USFWS or NMFS in order to ensure that activities they fund, authorize, permit, or carry out are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of the species or result in destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat. The ESA allows USFWS (terrestrial and some aquatic species) or NMFS (marine species) to allow takes that would otherwise be prohibited, provided that such taking is incidental to, and not the purpose of, carrying out an otherwise lawful activity ("incidental take"), by permit and an accompanying habitat conservation plan (USFWS only). In addition to the protection offered by listing, many species in Hawai'i have designated critical habitat, including most of the listed plants, the Blackburn's sphinx moth (Manduca blackburni), the palila (Loxioides bailleui), Hawaiian monk seal (Monachus schauinslandi), and the O'ahu 'elepaio (Chasiempis ibidis). Subspecies and other populations may be listed separately if they are sufficiently distinct from their conspecific relatives. In Hawai'i, such protections extend to bats, some birds, and many plants. Candidate species are those species which are under consideration for listing as threatened or endangered by the USFWS. NMFS calls these "species of concern" when there is not enough information available to decide on a listing or they are not actively being considered. A number of species are candidates or species of concern in Hawai'i.
The ESA also authorizes federal implementation of CITES.

## Marine Mammal Protection Act

The Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 protects marine mammals by prohibiting the take, harassment, and importation of marine mammals in the United States and by prohibiting the take of marine mammals by U.S. citizens anywhere in the world.
Exceptions can be granted for scientific research, education, native subsistence, and take incidental to commercial fisheries. The Act also requires establishing stock assessments and research. Species which fall below their "optimal sustainable population" size are listed as "depleted". Depleted populations must have a conservation plan to guide research and management actions to restore the health of the species.

## The Clean Water Act

The Clean Water Act of 1977 established the basic structure for regulating discharges of pollutants into the waters of the United States. Its goal is to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the nation's waters.
