## Seabirds

## 'Akē'akē or Bandrumped Storm Petrel

Hydrobates castro cryptoleucura

## SPECIES STATUS:

Hawaii Distinct Population Segment (DPS)
Federal Listed as Endangered, State Listed as Endangered, State Recognized as Indigenous, NatureServe Heritage Rank G4 -Apparently Secure, Regional Seabird Conservation Plan -USFWS 2005

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

The 'akē'akē or band-rumped storm-petrel is a medium sized, highly pelagic storm-petrel (Family: Hydrobatidae), and is the smallest and rarest seabird that breeds in Hawai'i. Adults are primarily blackish-brown and have a sharply defined narrow white band across rump area. Flight is characterized by shallow wing beats and long glides just over the surface of the ocean. Foraging alone or with conspecifics, 'akē'akē feed while sitting on the water or by dipping prey while flapping just above the ocean surface, often pattering water with feet. There is no diet information from Hawai'i, but elsewhere diet primarily consists of small fish, squid, and some crustaceans. Breeding biology in Hawai'i is poorly known, but these birds are known to nest in burrows or natural cavities in a variety of high-elevation, inland habitats. As with most seabirds, a single egg is laid per season. In 
Hawai'i, eggs
 are laid between May and June, and nestlings fledge in October. 'Akē'akē likely do not breed until they are three to seven years old, and likely live for 15 to 20 years. DISTRIBUTION: Historically, was abundant and widespread throughout Main Hawaiian Islands (MHI). Nesting colonies occur on Kaua'i at elevations around 600 meters 
(1,950 feet)
, on windward Lānaʻi around 610 meters (2000 feet), on Maui (in and around Haleakalā National Park) and, historically, in Ahihi-Kenaʻu Natural Area Reserve, and the island of 
Hawai'i (in Hawai'i
 Volcanoes National Park at elevations greater than 
1,200 meters (3,900 feet)
 and generally between 6,000 to 10,000 ft, and on Lehua. Outside of Hawai'i, the species nests in Japan and on the Galapagos, and on several islands in the Atlantic. At sea, they occur in the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.

## ABUNDANCE:

In Hawai'i, breeding population size is unknown, but likely very small. The breeding population on 
Kaua'
i was estimated at between 171 and 221 breeding pairs in 2002. Worldwide population is unknown, but likely less than 25,000 breeding pairs.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Breeds in a variety of remote, highelevation, inland habitats. On Kaua'i, colonies are in steep valleys vegetated with shrubs and grasses. On Maui and the island of Hawai'i, colonies occur on high, barren lava flows. Nesting in burrows or crevices in rock or lava has also been documented using artificial nest boxes. 

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

Tristram's storm-petrel is a large storm-petrel (Family: Hydrobatidae) with long, pointed wings, and a notched tail. Adult males and females are entirely brownish-gray. Flight is typical of storm-petrels, gliding low over water searching for food. Forages alone or with conspecifics, and typically forages at night. Tristram's storm-petrel feeds by dipping prey from the ocean's surface on the wing, often pattering the water with feet. In Hawai'i, diet includes fish, squid, coelenterates, crustaceans, and insects. Tristram's stormpetrels are winter breeders, and are nocturnal at nesting colonies. Nests are placed in recesses in rocks, under piles of mined guano, or burrows that they excavate under vegetation. Eggs are laid between December through February and nestlings fledge by June. Little information on parental care of egg or young. Like most storm petrels, age at first breeding is likely three to five years and individuals likely live between 15 and 20 years.

## DISTRIBUTION:

Tristram's storm-petrels breed on Nihoa and on all NWHI except for Midway and Kure atolls, although they historically bred on both as well as on MHI. Outside of Hawai'i, breeding colonies only occur on three small Japanese islands. Outside the breeding season, Tristram's storm-petrels range across the subtropical central and western Pacific Ocean.

## ABUNDANCE:

In Hawai'i, breeding colonies are estimated at less than 10,000 pairs, with the largest populations occurring on Nihoa (2,000 -3,000 pairs), Laysan (500 -2,000 pairs), and Pearl and Hermes Reef (1,000 -2,000 pairs). Between 2018-2022, a translocation project brought tristram's storm petrel chicks from the NWHI to the James Campbell National Wildlife Refuge on Oahu to create new protected breeding colonies safe from climate change. Worldwide population unknown.
LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT: Terrestrial: Islands in Hawai'i and Japan, which include both low-lying coralline sand islands and high volcanic islands. For nesting, prefers recesses in rock scree, under mined guano piles, or burrows excavated under vegetation. Marine: Pelagic.

## THREATS:

• Introduced predators: Like all seabirds, adults and nests are susceptible to predation by

## THREATS:

• Introduced predators: Like all seabirds, adults and nests are susceptible to predation by rats (Rattus spp.), and feral cats (Felis silvestris). All sites in NWHI are free of rats and cats. • Human disturbance: Pākalakala (gray-backed terns) are sensitive to nest disturbance, and flush from nests when humans approach. Exposed eggs and chicks are vulnerable to predation by 'iwa or great figatebirds (Fregata minor), 'akekeke or ruddy turnstones (Arenaria interpres), kioea or bristle-thighed curlews (Numenius tahitiensis), and Laysan (Telespiza cantans) and Nihoa (T. ultima) finches. • Manmade structures: On Kure, collisions with man-made structures have resulted in mortality.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The following management goals are important to Pacific seabird conservation: maintain, protect, and enhance habitat; eradicate or control non-natives; minimize bycatch and other negative effects of fishing; improve the effectiveness of oil spill response efforts; identify contaminates and hazardous substances; and minimize the effects of powerlines, towers, wind turbines and lights 
(USFWS 2005)
. The goal of these management actions is not only to protect seabird populations and their breeding colonies, but also to reestablish former breeding colonies thereby reducing the risk of extinction. In addition to these efforts, future management specific to Hawaiian populations of pākalakala (gray-backed terns) should include the following:
• Eradicate cats, mice (Mus musculus), and rats from islets off MHI.
• Protect colonies from human disturbance.
• Continue protection and management of wildlife sanctuaries and refuges.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.
RESEARCH PRIORITIES: Most research priorities for seabirds are related to determining the most appropriate methods for achieving the above goals. Research priorities specific to the pākalakala (gray-backed tern) include the following:
• Long-term demographic studies are needed to determine population trends, survival rates, and reproductive success.

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

The noio or black noddy is a medium-sized, abundant, and gregarious tern (Family: Laridae) with a pantropical distribution. Seven noio (black noddy) subspecies are generally recognized, and two are resident in Hawai'i: A. s. melanogenys (MHI) and A. s. marcusi (NWHI). Individuals have slender wings, a wedge-shaped tail, and black bill which is slightly decurved. Adult males and females are sooty black with a white cap and have reddish brown to bright orange legs and feet; bill droops slightly. Flight is swift with rapid wing beats and usually direct and low over the ocean; this species almost never soars high. Often forages in large, mixed species flocks associated with schools of large predatory fishes which drive prey species to the surface. Noio (black noddy) generally forage in nearshore waters and feeds mainly by dipping the surface from the wing or by making shallow dives. Opportunistic, in Hawai'i, noio (black noddy) primarily takes juvenile goatfish, lizardfish, herring, flyingfish, and gobies. Nests in large, dense colonies that include non-breeding juvenile birds. Established pairs return to the same nest site year after year. Breeding is highly variable and egg laying occurs year-round. Both parents incubate single egg, and brood and feed chick. Birds first breed at two to three years of age, and the oldest known individual was 25 years old.
DISTRIBUTION: Noio (black noddy) breed throughout the Hawaiian Archipelago, including all islands of NWHI and the coastal cliffs, sea caves and offshore islets of MHI. Outside of Hawai'i, noio (black noddy) breed on islands throughout the world's tropical oceans. Noio (black noddy) typically remain near (within 80 kilometers [50 miles]) their breeding colonies yearround.

## ABUNDANCE:

In Hawai'i, population estimated at 12,000 breeding pairs with the largest populations occurring on Midway Atoll (6,000 pairs) and Nihoa (5,000 pairs). Worldwide population is estimated at 1,000,000 to 1,500,000 breeding pairs.
LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT: Terrestrial: Noio (black noddy) breed on oceanic and offshore islands, both on low-lying coralline sand islands and high volcanic islands. In Hawai'i, noio (black noddy) place their nests on ledges and in crevices of coastal cliffs, in sea caves, and in ironwood (Casuarina spp.) trees. Marine: Nearshore waters.

## THREATS:

Marine: Nearshore waters.

## THREATS:

• Introduced predators: Like all seabirds, adults and nests are susceptible to predation by rats (Rattus spp.), and feral cats (Felis silvestris). All sites in NWHI are free of rats and cats. • Native predators: On Nihoa and Laysan, native finches (Telespiza spp.) are responsible for considerable egg mortality.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The following management goals are important to Pacific seabird conservation: maintain, protect, and enhance habitat; eradicate or control non-natives; minimize bycatch and other negative effects of fishing; improve the effectiveness of oil spill response efforts; identify contaminates and hazardous substances; and minimize the effects of powerlines, towers, wind turbines and lights 
(USFWS 2005)
. The goal of these management actions is not only to protect seabird populations and their breeding colonies, but also to reestablish former breeding colonies thereby reducing the risk of extinction. In addition to these efforts, future management specific to Hawaiian populations of blue-gray noddy should include the following:
• Continue protection and management of wildlife sanctuaries and refuges.
• Conduct social attraction to protected areas in the MHI.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.
RESEARCH PRIORITIES: Most research priorities for seabirds are related to determining the most appropriate methods for achieving the above goals. Research priorities specific to the blue gray-noddy include the following:
• Development and implementation of standardized survey protocols to determine current population size and status.

## Seabirds 'Ā or Brown Booby Sula leucogaster

Photo: USFWS SPECIES STATUS: State recognized as Indigenous, State NatureServe Heritage Rank G5 -Secure, North American Waterbird Conservation Plan -Moderate concern, Regional Seabird Conservation Plan -USFWS 2005

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

The 'ā or brown booby is a large, striking seabird (Family: Sulidae) with a pantropical distribution. Four 'ā (brown booby) subspecies are recognized, and two (S. l. plotus & S.l. brewsteri) are resident in Hawai'i. Individuals have long pointed wings and a relatively short, wedge-shaped tail. Adult males and females are overall dark brown, with white belly and underwings with a sharp demarcation across lower breast between the white of belly and brown of neck. Large bill and legs and feet are yellow in females and grayish-green in males; females are larger than males. Flight is characterized by strong flapping interspersed with gliding. Will forage alone, but most often forages in large, mixed species flocks associated with schools of large predatory fishes which drive prey species to the surface. 'Ā (brown booby) generally forages in nearshore waters and captures prey by plunge-diving from one to 15 meters (3 -50 feet) above the water, often remaining underwater for 25 to 40 seconds. In Hawai'i, diet is comprised of flying fish, squid, mackerel scad, juvenile goatfish, and anchovy.
Nest in small colonies of tens to hundreds of pairs and most return to natal colony to breed. 'Ā (brown booby) is the only ground nesting booby that builds a nest, and its construction is an important part of courtship. Nests are constructed from whatever is available including branches, seabird bones, and human debris. Unlike most seabirds, 'ā (brown booby) typically lays two eggs per breeding season. The eggs hatch asynchronously, and the first chick to hatch usually pushes the other sibling out of the nest. In Hawai'i, peak egg laying occurs between March and May and chicks fledge by September. Both parents incubate eggs and brood and feed chicks. Adults continue to feed young up to 37 weeks after fledging. Birds first breed at four to five years of age and the oldest known individual was 26 years old.
DISTRIBUTION: 'Ā (brown booby) breed throughout the NWHI and in MHI on offshore islets (e.g., Moku Manu, Lehua), on Moku Mana at Pauwalu Point Seabird Sanctuary on Maui, and possibly on the island of O'ahu on the cliffs of Ulupa'u Head at the Kāne'ohe Bay Marine Corps Base. Outside of Hawai'i, 'ā (brown booby) breed on islands in the tropical waters of the Pacific, Indian, and Atlantic oceans, the Caribbean and Red seas, and seas north of Australia. Little is known about movements and distribution outside the breeding season.

## ABUNDANCE:

In Hawai'i, population estimated at 1,400 breeding pairs with the largest population occurring on Lehua. Worldwide population estimate for S. l. plotus is 50,000 to 70,000 breeding pairs.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

To protect the ability of wintering kōlea to survive while in Hawai'i and to return in good condition to breeding grounds in Alaska, current statewide and island-specific conservation actions should include:
• Protection of current habitat.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.
RESEARCH PRIORITIES: Kōlea studies remain fragmentary, probably because the species is neither endemic nor endangered. Research priorities should include the following:
• Increased study of all aspects of ecology and behavior of kōlea in Hawai'i, and comparative research on unstudied populations elsewhere. • Evaluation of conditions on winter range habitats as related to expanding human activities (e.g., agriculture, reclamation, urbanization, pollution). • Increased effort to make accurate population estimates, along with systematic monitoring wherever possible to facilitate the recognition of trends and potential problems.

THREATS: Primary threats include the following:

• Avian disease.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

To protect the ability of wintering koloa māpu to survive while in Hawai'i and to return in good condition to breeding grounds in North America, statewide and island-specific conservation actions should include:
• Protection of current habitat.
• Protection and restoration of additional wetland habitat, especially where it can be reclaimed from abandoned urban or agricultural uses.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

Only one published study of visiting koloa māpu has been undertaken, probably in part because of their annual presence and numbers are uncertain.
Research priorities should include the following:
• Better understanding of habitat needs and preferences, including foraging and population limiting factors. • Population reactions to habitat modifications, changes in food availability, and competition with other migrants. • Life-history and population dynamics in wintering areas.
• Better understanding of geographic relationship between nesting areas and wintering areas.
• Make-up of local populations relative to survival and condition during winter.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

To protect the ability of wintering hunakai to survive while in Hawai'i and to return in good condition to breeding grounds in North America, statewide and island-specific conservation actions should include:
• Protection of current habitat.
• Protection and restoration of additional habitat.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.
RESEARCH PRIORITIES: Hunakai have been only minimally studied. Research priorities should include the following:
• Better understanding of habitat requirements and behavioral plasticity, to improve assessments of probable responses to coastal (beach) development, habitat degradation, pollution, and other human disturbances. • Increased understanding of movements of individuals that overfly the Hawaiian Islands, support needed studies of the extent to which distinct breeding populations exist and whether migration routes and wintering areas are population-specific.

. In The Birds of North America, No. 653 (Poole A, Gill F, editors). Philadelphia, (PA): The Academy of Natural Sciences; and Washington DC: The American Ornithologists' Union.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

To protect the ability of wintering 'ūlili to survive while in Hawai'i and to return in good condition to breeding grounds in North America, statewide and island-specific conservation actions should include:
• Protection of current habitat.
• Protection and restoration of additional wetland habitat, especially where it can be reclaimed from abandoned urban or agricultural uses.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.
RESEARCH PRIORITIES: 'Ūlili have been only minimally studied. Research priorities should include the following:
• Basic research on demography in wintering habitat.
• More information about population sizes and trends, and population regulation.
• Better understanding of habitat needs and preferences, including foraging needs, population limiting factors, and adaptation to modified wintering habitats and how they affect migration routes. • Increased understanding of movements of individuals that overfly the Hawaiian Islands.
THREATS: Primary threats include the following:
• Loss of wetland habitat to development.
• Degradation of habitat due to pollution, hydrology alteration, or invasions by alien species.
• West Nile virus or other avian diseases.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

To protect the ability of wintering American wigeons to survive while in Hawai'i and to return in good condition to breeding grounds in North America, statewide and island-specific conservation actions should include:
• Protection of current habitat.
• Protection and restoration of additional wetland habitat, especially where it can be reclaimed from abandoned urban or agricultural uses.
MONITORING: Continue surveys of population and distribution in known and likely habitats.
RESEARCH PRIORITIES: Little study of visiting wigeons has been undertaken, probably in part because of their annual presence and numbers are uncertain. Research priorities should include the following:
• Better understanding of habitat needs and preferences, including foraging and population limiting factors. • Increased understanding of movements of individuals that overfly the Hawaiian Islands.

## Hawaiian Land snails

Family Succineidae Only 29 species are known to be extant 
(Yeung and Hayes 2018)
. These snails range in size from approximately 5-12 mm and are both arboreal and ground dwelling and lay large gelatinous egg masses. Locally, these snails are known as "Snot in a Hat," because their large body often does not fit inside their small-flat shells. These are some of the most commonly observed snails along upper elevation hiking trails.
DISTRIBUTION: Members of this family are all single-island endemics with species historically occurring on all main Hawaiian Islands.

## ABUNDANCE:

The entire family is experiencing range reductions and extinctions across their range.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Key habitat for this family is native wet and mesic forests, with some species occurring in coastal strand.

## THREATS:

The most urgent threats come from climate change impacts such as fire and drier conditions, loss of habitat due to habitat-altering weeds and ungulates, and most devastatingly direct predation by introduced predators such as rats (Rattus spp.), Euglandina spp., and Jackson's chameleons (Chamaeleo jacksonii) 
(Schalie 1969
, Clarke et al. 1984
, Hadfield 1986
, Cowie 2001
, Holland et al. 2008
, Meyer et al 2017)
. Although it has not been observed in Achatinelline habitat, the New Guinea flatworm platydemus manokwari, has been introduced to the islands and has been documented in lower elevation habitats. This flatworm is a molluscivore and has caused devastating declines of native snail populations in other areas of the Pacific 
(Gerlach et al. 2020)
. Additionally, pathogens and parasites are thought to be impacting some populations, but more research is needed to confirm (Personal Communication with David Sischo).

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

• Survey across their range for undiscovered populations.
• Conduct phylogenetic assessments to confirm species identify and the phylogenetic relationships to other populations and species. As well as to assess the potential maintenance of genetic diversity and the reduction of inbreeding impacts. • Conduct stop-gap predator control where possible to reduce impacts from introduced predators. Actions include rat trapping and the manual removal of Euglandina spp. and individuals between cages and between facilities to hedge against extinction.

Fornax: 4 sp.The superfamily Elateroidea includes click beetles, fireflies, and their relatives. In Hawaiʻi it is represented by two families, Elateridae (true click beetles) and Eucnemidae (false click beetles). Both groups are capable of engaging a mechanism at the junction of the pro-and mesosterna to snap the body with an audible click, as a defense and to flip themselves over. The larvae of all species are found in dead rotting wood, where they may be detritivores or predators. All three elaterid genera (Dacnitus, Eopenthes, and Itodacnus) are strictly endemic to Hawaiʻi. Eopenthes is the largest and most common, with 34 species. The 11 known species of Itodacnus are rarer, except for one species frequently found on Kauaʻi. Dacnitus is represented by a single species that has apparently not been seen since the 1800s. Among the eucnemids, Dromaeolus are by far the most diverse and abundant, though still rare; typically one or two individuals are found per Malaise trap sample. Forty-nine species are known, but most from only one or two specimens, and there are probably more undescribed. The four native Fornax species are all extremely rare, last collected in 1965, and the monotypic Epiphanis is only known from the original collections in 1895.

## DISTRIBUTION:

Click beetles are known from all the MHI except Kahoʻolawe and Niʻihau, and two Itodacnus are found on Necker and Nihoa.

## ABUNDANCE:

Unknown. A lack of systematic surveys prevents accurate population estimates. However, the loss and degradation of native habitats likely means species within the superfamily are declining. Larvae are cryptic in dead wood and adults are active for a relatively brief period in the summer, so they may be underrepresented by traditional survey methods. Eopenthes may be collected by sweeping and Dromaeolus in Malaise traps, but both are still rare. Arciellia, Asyndetus, Diaphorus, Hydrophorus, Major, Medetera, Paraliancalus: 1-3 spp. each The long-legged flies are a highly diverse group in Hawaiʻi. The largest genus is Campsicnemus, with over 200 species described to date. It is the second largest radiation of endemic flies in Hawaiʻi, and the sixth largest overall. They are particularly notable for the modification and ornamentation of the male legs (usually the middle one), which is used in courtship. They are generalist predators of small arthropods such as springtails and mites and inhabit a variety of forest habitats. Color is correlated to general habitat preference: species found on leaf litter are typically dull brown, water skaters are shiny brown to black, and those that prefer live leaves are metallic green to blue. A complex of genera formerly lumped under Eurynogaster, including Adachia, Arciellia, Elmoia, Major, Sigmatineurum, Swezeyella, and Uropachys contains similar but larger species with less elaborate male ornamentation. Most are distributed generally in forests, but Sigmatineurum and Major are specialists in aquatic habitats, found at seeps, waterfalls, and cascades. In contrast, the species of Conchopus are found only at the coast, on wave-washed rocks, and Hydrophorus are found around brackish coastal and lowland ponds.

## DISTRIBUTION:

Long-legged flies are known from all the Main Hawaiian Islands except Niʻihau and Kahoʻolawe. The coastal Hydrophorus and Conchopus are also found in the NWHI.

## ABUNDANCE:

Unknown. A lack of systematic surveys prevents any population estimate. Some species are common and abundant, while others are rarely seen and known from only a handful of specimens. Some of latter may be infrequently collected due specialized habitats rather than inherent rarity. Little is known about the habitat requirements of specific species, particularly for immature stages, and the loss of native habitats likely means that some species are declining.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

The breeding host of Drosophila musaphilia is Acacia koa, where larvae feed in fermenting sap fluxes. Acacia koa is abundant and reproducing at all sites where D. musaphilia is found, suggesting that unlike other rare Drosophila, its numbers may not be strictly host-limited at the sites where it occurs. It appears to be extremely limited in range compared to the broad distribution of Acacia koa, suggesting limiting due to either non-host factors or in the extent of suitable conditions for sap fluxes.
Introduced saprophagous invertebrates may also affect breeding habitat quality.

## THREATS:

 Habitat loss and degradation due to invasive plants and insects, disturbance by non-native ungulates, and fire from nearby agriculture and recreational activity.  Non-native predators, including ants and wasps (Vespula pensylvanica).  Insufficient information hampers conservation efforts.

 Miridae is a large and diverse family, with a correspondingly large number of endemic lineages. Most species feed on plants, hence the common name plant bugs; however, some are predaceous, and for many natives the life history is unknown. There are three large radiations: Nesiomiris, Orthotylus, and Sarona. All three are highly host-specific, with each species restricted to single islands. Nesiomiris is unusual in that all 50 species are found only on a few hosts in Araliaceae (Cheirodendron spp. and Polyscias spp.) and Aquifoliaceae (Ilex anomala), with multiple species often found sympatrically. Orthotylus are found on a wide variety of host plants in at least 18 families; a few are found on multiple plants and may be predaceous. Sarona occur on a few of the same hosts as Orthotylus, but most are on different plants, especially Melicope. The remaining genera are much smaller and have varied habits; Engytatus, Loulucoris, and Sulamita are host-specific plant feeders, while the others are found in a variety of situations and may be generalists or predaceous. Hyalopeplus pellucidus is remarkable for an endemic insect in being a generalist herbivore found in a wide range of habitats from dry coastal strands to montane wet forests. H. pelucidus seems to be able to survive in the presence of invasive predatory ants, but this cannot be said for other native plant bugs. Nesidiorchestes is a peculiar group of flightless jumping bugs found in leaf litter. Undescribed species are known at least for Kamehameha, Koanoa, Nesidiorchestes, and Sulamita, but comprehensive revisions are required to determine exactly how many there are. 

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

 Conduct studies to document the biology, habitat requirements, and life histories of these species.  Initiate studies to determine current distributions of known endemic species.  Initiate efforts to locate and identify new species.  Initiate studies to determine the effects of non-native predators and parasitoids on species.  Conduct and support systematic and taxonomic assessments of poorly known and understudied taxa. Planthoppers in the family Delphacidae are a large and diverse group worldwide. They are easily distinguished from other families by the large moveable spur at the apex of the hind tibia. The endemic genera have diverse habits; almost all are strongly host-plant specific. Emoloana belongs to a different subfamily from the other genera and feeds on native grasses. Dictyophorodelphax is a striking endemic genus with a long horn on the head; all species feed on native ʻakoko (Euphorbiaceae: Euphorbia). The two species of Nesodryas feed on monocots. The remaining genera feed on a wide variety of wet to mesic forest trees and shrubs, with a high diversity of hosts within each. Nesosydne is by far the most diverse genus, with many undescribed species.

## DISTRIBUTION:

Delphacids are known from all the Main Hawaiian Islands except Niʻihau and Kahoʻolawe. Several species of Emoloana are also known from Laysan in the NWHI.

## ABUNDANCE:

Unknown. A lack of systematic surveys prevents any population estimate. However, the loss of native habitats likely means that species within the family are declining with populations occurring in dry and mesic forests are believed to be declining rapidly. A large number of species of Nesosydne have not been collected in many years and may be very rare or extinct. Emoloana is especially vulnerable as it is restricted to native grasses which are increasingly rare.

DISTRIBUTION: Hylaeus anthracinus is found from Hawaiʻi to Oʻahu and was formerly one of the most widely distributed native bees. While it is still known to occur on all islands in that range except Lānaʻi, the loss of native coastal vegetation has caused the occupied area to contract dramatically. It can still be found along several long stretches of coastline on the northwest coast of Hawaiʻi in South Kohala and North Kona, sometimes in extremely high densities. Elsewhere on the island, it is known only from a single, very small population near South Point, and from a reintroduced population at Puʻuhonua O Hōnaunau National Historical Park in South Kona (there is one high-elevation record at Pōhakuloa from 2004, but it has not found there since and it is unknown if there is a breeding population there). On Maui and Molokaʻi, it has been found at only two sites, though much of the coast is unexplored. Three sites are known for Oʻahu, where population numbers have seriously declined since 2011 with the spread of an alien yellow-faced bee from India, Hylaeus strenuus. , and hundreds more remain undescribed, making them the second largest endemic radiation in Hawaiʻi (flies in the family Drosophilidae being the largest). The group is divided into two subgenera, Hyposmocoma sensu stricto, where the caterpillars make cases (205 species), and Euperissus, where the caterpillars live freely (158 species; 
Zimmerman, 1978)
. As caterpillars they are mostly herbivorous, feeding on leaves, ferns, plant debris, and lichens. However, some species are predatory on insects and even snails, which is extremely rare among Lepidoptera 
(Rubinoff and Haines, 2005)
. They inhabit a wide range of habitats, from the coast to montane wet forests and barren lava flows. Some are aquatic or semi-aquatic, grazing on moss and algae on rocks of permanent or intermittent streams. Due to the large size of the group, small size of individual specimens, and many cryptic species, identification is often difficult, especially without both the larval case and the adult.
DISTRIBUTION: Hyposmocoma are known from all the MHI and the NWHI.

## ABUNDANCE:

As a group unknown. A lack of systematic surveys prevents accurate population estimates, and their small size, large number of undescribed species, and lack of literature resources make the species difficult to identify. The loss of native habitats likely means that species within the genus are declining, particularly those that inhabit specialized niches. However, at least some of the case-making species are able to persist at disturbed lowland sites with few other native species.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Hyposmocoma occur in all native habitats from sea level to alpine deserts. Host material is widely varied and includes native plants, lichens, algae, and mosses. Some species are predatory on insects or snails.

## THREATS:

 Habitat loss and degradation due to conversion for agriculture, logging, grazing, and soil disturbance by a suite of non-native ungulates, and the introduction of invasive plants.  Loss of native host plants. 

## GENERAL INFORMATION:

The family Crambidae includes 137 described native species which feed on a variety of native plants. The most species-rich crambid genus is Eudonia, containing more than 60 described species, and likely many more undescribed species. Caterpillars of many Eudonia species feed on mosses and lichens and can be common, even in relatively disturbed areas. Other large lineages in this family include Udea (44 spp.), Mestolobes (34 spp.), and Omiodes (23 spp.). Caterpillars of Udea and Mestolobes feed on a variety of native plants, while most Omiodes feed on monocots, including grasses, sedges, palms, and lilies. Most crambid moths are nocturnal, but many Mestolobes are active during the day, and are frequently seen visiting flowers. Crambid moths, like other native lepidoptera, are likely important pollinators for native plants.
DISTRIBUTION: Crambid moths are known from all the MHI and the NWHI.

## ABUNDANCE:

As a group unknown. A lack of systematic surveys prevents accurate population estimates. However, the loss of native habitats likely means that species within the order are declining. Several species of Omiodes have not been seen in over 100 years and are likely extinct.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Crambid moths occur in all native habitats from sea level to alpine deserts. Host material is widely varied and includes native flowering plants, mosses, and lichens.

## THREATS:

 Habitat loss and degradation due to conversion for agriculture, logging, grazing, and soil disturbance by a suite of non-native ungulates, and the introduction of invasive plants.  Loss of native host plants.  Insufficient information, especially for rare species, hampers conservation efforts.  Non-native species, including ants (Formicidae), especially the big-headed ant (Pheidole megacephala), and several species of parasitic flies (Diptera) and wasps (Hymenoptera) attack both larvae and adult moths. Both are larval food specialists. Caterpillars of the Kamehameha butterfly feed on native plants in the nettle family (Urticaceae), primarily māmaki (Pipturus spp.) but also ʻakolea (Boehmeria grandis), ʻolonā (Touchardia latifolia) and ʻōpuhe (T. sandwicensis), while those of Blackburn's blue feed on koa (Acacia koa) and ʻaʻaliʻi (Dodonaea viscosa). Using only koa and ʻaʻaliʻi as host plants is somewhat unusual for insects since these plants are unrelated. Interestingly, though, koa and ʻaʻaliʻi are also the two host plants of the koa bug (Coleotichus blackburniae).

## DISTRIBUTION:

The Kamehameha butterfly is known from all of the Main Hawaiian Islands except Kahoʻolawe. Blackburn's blue is known from all of the Main Hawaiian Islands.

## ABUNDANCE:

Unknown. A lack of systematic surveys prevents accurate population estimates. However, the loss of native habitats likely means that the species are declining. The Kamehameha butterfly has been increasingly less abundant over the past 30 years, particularly on Oʻahu where it is rarely seen in the Koʻolau range. Captive rearing and reintroductions of the Kamehameha butterfly were attempted by DLNR-DOFAW from 2016 to 2020 in the southern Koʻolau Range of Oʻahu but were not successful due to high predation rates on caterpillars. Blackburn's blue appears to be fairly common but has not been studied as much.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Both butterflies occur in native dry to wet forests.

## PLANTS SPECIES OF GREATEST CONSERVATION NEED WORKHORSE SPECIES and IMPORTANT INTERACTIONS SPECIES INFORMATION:

The plant species listed below are important components of the native plant communities that provide habitat for native wildlife. They are also important plant species for post-fire rehabilitation, ecosystem restoration, pollinator habitat, and coastal hardening.
DISTRIBUTION: These species are indigenous or endemic to Hawaiʻi and have broad distributions across the state and throughout most ecosystems from sea level to sub-alpine habitats.

## ABUNDANCE:

These plant species are relatively abundant compared to rare species. They are not listed as Threatened or Endangered and are not targets for the Plant Extinction Prevention Program. Instead, they are important foundations for plant communities and are moderately abundant. Some taxa are locally-abundant in remnant native habitat, but otherwise absent from developed and degraded areas.

## THREATS:

• Browsing and habitat destruction by feral animals;
• Herbivory and/or seed predation by small vertebrate pests;
• Competition from invasive non-native plants;
• Landslides, hurricanes, wildfire, or other geologic events;
• Human disturbance;
• Disease;
• Damaging herbivory by invasive non-native invertebrate pests;
• Loss of native pollinators or other mutualists;

## THREATS:

• Habitat degradation results from water diversion, stream channelization, dams, pollution, the introduction of exotic species and parasites, and climate change. Water diversion, stream channelization, and dams result in habitat degradation through altered stream flows, which also causes a loss of riparian vegetation, shelter and erosion control; higher water temperatures; and lower dissolved oxygen levels. 'O'opu naniha are not as threatened by altered streams as other Hawaiian gobies, although reduced water flows still can limit larvae from reaching the ocean and recruiting back into streams; • Non-point source water pollution, such as nutrients, sedimentation, and chemicals may threaten ʻoʻopu naniha; however, the consequence of these pollutants is relatively unknown and needs to be further studied; • Introduction of exotic species, diseases and parasites such as tilapia are significant threats to ʻoʻopu naniha. Historical introductions of game fish and more recent unwanted exotic fish from the aquarium trade are both problems. These exotic fish species prey on native fish, outcompete native fish for food, and spread parasites and diseases; • Fishing for ʻoʻopu naniha occurs and could become a more severe threat in combination with the above threats.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The goals of conservation actions are to not only protect current populations, but to also establish further populations to reduce the risk of extinction. Past actions to restore fish populations have consisted of a ban on gill, drag, draw, and seine netting; stream cleanup efforts, and public outreach. In addition to common state-wide and island conservation actions, specific actions include:
• Improve altered streams;
• Restore riparian vegetation to help decrease instream heating and reduce sediment loads;
• Remove alien species;
• Create pools in frequently dewatered stretches to provide safe usable habitat between flows; • Collaborate with the Commission on Water Resources Management and the Land Board to ensure adequate Instream Flow and biological integrity of riparian areas; • Work to clean streams with significant pollution;
• Continue developing GIS database and making it web-accessible; • Use science-based management of recreational fishing;
• Increase education and outreach efforts, particularly on issues of fishing-related life history, water pollution, and how to deal with unwanted aquarium pets; • Continue on-going partnerships focused on environmental and fisheries education and conservation and expand partnerships.

• Habitat Connectivity: Evaluate stream flow continuity and barrier removal.

Freshwater Invertebrates

## Hīhīwai and Hapawai

Neritina granosa Neritina vespertine

## SPECIES STATUS:

Endemic IUCN Red List -Not Considered SPECIES INFORMATION: These fresh and brackish water snails grow to about four centimeters (two inches) in length. Hīhīwai (N. granosa) are more active and more visible at night. Both species graze on algae growing on hard substrates. Eggs are deposited in capsules about two millimeters (one-tenth of an inch) long that are attached to rocks or other shells. Each capsule has about 250 eggs. Most egg-laying occurs from June through August. After hatching, the larvae wash into the ocean where they develop planktonically. Hīhīwai larvae develop in the ocean for up to a year before moving back into freshwater or estuaries to live out their lives. The young snails can be seen moving upstream in summer in single file along the rocks when they are about two to three millimeters (one-tenth of an inch) in size. Hapawai (N. vespertina) have only a few months developing in the ocean before they recruit to estuaries and ponds, and rarely to streams. Recruitment peaks shortly after rains. Hīhīwai may serve as good indicator species for stream quality. Hīhīwai shells from low elevations differ in shape from those at higher elevations and flows.
DISTRIBUTION: Historically, they were found on all the main islands. Currently, hapawai can still be found on all the main islands in disturbed and undisturbed streams, but hīhīwai are only common in high quality streams and are rare on O'ahu.

## ABUNDANCE:

Their abundance is lower than it was historically in all but the most remote streams.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Hīhīwai occur more in well-oxygenated lower to middle reaches of streams. They prefer streams with boulders and coarse gravel substrates. Hapawai occur in the lower reaches of streams and extend more into the estuary.

## THREATS:

• Both species have been used by Hawaiians as a food source, though hīhīwai are preferred; • Stream channelization and burial, pollution, and water diversions have affected the distribution and abundance of these snails. In particular, hīhīwai are limited in their upstream migration by low stream flows and in-stream obstructions.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The goals of conservation actions are to not only protect current populations, but to also establish further populations to reduce the risk of extinction. In addition to common statewide and island conservation actions, specific actions include:

## Marine Mammals

## Īlio-holo-i-ka-uaua or Hawaiian monk seal

Neomonachus schauinslandi 

## ABUNDANCE:

The total population is estimated at 1,600 individuals, most of which occur in the NWHI, with a decreasing population trend. About 400 of these seals occur in the MHI, where the population is increasing.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Hawaiian monk seals feed primarily in waters around atolls and islands throughout the NWHI and MHI, including within lagoon systems and on reef slopes, submarine ridges and seamounts. Terrestrial habitat is used about one-third of the time and includes haul-out areas for pupping, nursing, molting and resting, primarily on sandy beaches, but virtually all substrates are used. Beach vegetation is used for protection from wind and rain. In 2015, NOAA expanded the critical habitat designation to parts of the MHI, extending protections to 200 meters in depth and 5 meters inland from the shoreline around islands like 
Kaula, Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Maui Nui, and Hawaiʻi Island (NOAA Fisheries, 2015)
.
rare and/or seasonal.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Minke, fin, and North Pacific right whales primarily inhabit coastal and shelf waters, but also can be found in offshore waters. Sei, Bryde's, and blue whales generally occur in coastal, shelf, and oceanic waters THREATS:
• Whaling. Population declines due to whaling occurred worldwide, although international limits on commercial whaling have greatly reduced this threat. • Boat strikes and entanglement. Ships colliding with baleen whales and entanglement in fishing gear are significant causes of injury and mortality. • Marine pollution and debris. Ingestion of marine debris can cause intestinal injury or blockage. Accumulations of tiny, plastic particles containing PCBs and DDEs can cause toxic effects when ingested; this may be particularly dangerous for baleen whales because they take in large quantities of water at a time during feeding. • Entanglement. Fishing gear poses a major threat to baleen whales, often leading to injury, impaired movement, reduced feeding ability, and sometimes death • Climate change. Climate change threatens baleen whales by altering their food availability, shifting migration patterns, and increasing exposure to harmful human activities such as ship traffic and fishing gear entanglement. • Underwater noise. Underwater detonations during military exercises and vessel noise may interfere with feeding and breeding behavior.
CONSERVATION ACTIONS: Actions specific to baleen whales include the continuation of the following:
• Increasing education and outreach to reduce vessel strikes.
• Reducing marine debris and pollutants in the marine environment.
• Collaborating with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on enforcement of the Marine Mammal Protection Act to prevent marine mammal harassment and disturbance.

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

Leatherback sea turtles are the largest of all sea turtle species and are easily identified by their unique, leathery shell without scales. They primarily feed on jellyfish and are known for their deep-diving ability. Little information exists on the feeding behavior of post-hatchling and juvenile leatherback sea turtles living in pelagic habitats, but most likely they are exclusively carnivorous. Leatherbacks are the only sea turtles in which adults are also pelagic and carnivorous, feeding on jellyfish, siphonophores, and salps, although they also feed on plants.
They exhibit rapid growth rates from hatchling to juvenile (approximately 32 centimeters in length per year). Reproduction is seasonal, with two to three years between nesting. ABUNDANCE: Rare in Hawai'i. The Pacific population is critically low, with a few thousand individuals remaining. Globally the annual number of breeding females is estimated at 34,000 to 36,000 nesting females, with significant declines in some populations.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Usually found in deep, highly productive waters. They occur in water that is far colder than that inhabited by any other sea turtle species.
Nesting does not occur in Hawai'i but occurs on sandy beaches in the subtropics and tropics.

## THREATS:

• Fisheries bycatch: Mortality of adult and juvenile turtles results from fisheries bycatch. CONSERVATION ACTIONS: Actions specific to leatherback sea turtles should include the following:
• International Cooperation: Global agreements to protect migratory routes and nesting sites.
• Fishing Gear Modifications: Use of turtle excluder devices (TEDs) to reduce bycatch.
• Protected Areas: Establishment of marine reserves and protection of nesting beaches.
• Public Awareness: Campaigns to reduce marine debris and illegal trade.

## Marine Fishes

## Hāpuʻupuʻu or Hawaiian grouper

## Hyporthodus quernus

Image Credit: Keoki Stender

## SPECIES STATUS:

IUCN Red List -Least Concern SPECIES INFORMATION: Hāpuʻupuʻu or the Hawaiian grouper is an endemic species of benthic finfish found throughout the Hawaiian archipelago and Johnston Atoll. Like many groupers, they are sequential protogynous hermaphrodites meaning that they can change from an initial female phase to a terminal male phase throughout their lives. Hāpuʻupuʻu are slow-growing and relatively long-lived, with specimens previously caught up to 50 years old, and an estimated maximum age of up to 76 years.
In Hawaiʻi, hāpuʻupuʻu are a prized foodfish caught almost exclusively by the deep-sea hook and line bottomfish fishery. Hāpuʻupuʻu are a relatively small component of the total main Hawaiian Island (MHI) Deep-7 bottomfish fishery at about 3% in recent years, and are today considered primarily an incidentally-caught species. The were however a primary component of the Northwest Hawaiian Island (NWHI) bottomfish fishery prior to its closure in 2009.

## DISTRIBUTION:

Hāpuʻupuʻu can be found throughout the Hawaiian archipelago as well as Johnston Atoll.

## ABUNDANCE:

Unknown. There is no current species-specific stock assessment for hāpuʻupuʻu. The species falls within the MHI Deep-7 bottomfish complex which also includes 'ōpakapaka (Pristipomoides filamentosus; pink snapper), onaga (Etelis coruscans; longtail snapper), ehu (Etelis carbunculus; ruby snapper), kalekale (Pristipomoides seiboldii; Von Siebold's snapper), gindai (Pristipomoides zonatus; oblique-banded snapper), and lehi (Aphareus rutilans; silverjaw snapper). The latest stock assessment published by NOAA Pacific Islands Fishery Science Center (PIFSC) in 2024 found the complex to be neither overfisher, nor experiencing overfishing.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Hāpuʻupuʻu depth preference has been noted to vary across its range, with fish found in progressively deeper waters with southern movement down the Hawaiian archipelago. This has previously been attributed to "tropical submergence," or the phenomenon in which species adapted to cooler water are restricted to greater depths in areas where shallow temperatures exceed their tolerances. Though hāpuʻupuʻu as a benthic species are known to be found on coral reef habitat within recreational dive depth limits fish in the NWHI, in the MHI they are most commonly known to utilize rocky habitat and structure beyond the mesophotic zone. fishes are small, secretive species that inhabit crevices, sand patches, and reef structures. Their coloration and behavior make them difficult to observe, yet they play vital roles in maintaining reef health by controlling algae and serving as prey for larger species. These are mostly small (less than 18 centimeters or seven inches) site-attached reef fishes. Decorated dragonets (Callionymus decoratus) reach 28 centimeters (eleven inches) in length as does Commerson's frogfish (Antennarius), and some of the scorpionfishes are also large. 'Upāpalu (Apogon) is a zooplanktivore. The blennies mostly feed on algae except for the Plagiotremus species which feed on mucus and skin tissue of other fishes. The callionymids (dragonets) and gobies are carnivorous on small invertebrates. The Hawaiian triplefin (Enneapterygius) is omnivorous. Commerson's frogfish (Antennarius) is a sit-and-wait predator using a modifield dorsal fin spine as a fishing lure. The scorpionfishes (Scorpaenidae) and lizardfishes (Synodontidae) are ambush predators of fishes and invertebrates. 'Upāpalu (Apogon) males brood young in their mouths until hatching. Male blennies and gobies of most species guard demersal eggs until hatching. Mainland's goby (Psilogobius) lives in commensal burrows with an alpheid shrimp and Oxyurichthys lonchotus may do the same. Hawaiian orbicular velvetfish (Caracanthus) may be a protogynous hermaphrodite. The species common names and Hawaiian names are: Apogon maculiferus (spotted cardinalfish, 'upāpalu), Cirrepecetes obscurus (gargantuan blenny, pao'o), Enchelyurus brunneolus (no common name), Entomacrodus marmoratus (marbled blenny, pao'o), Entomacrodus strasburgi (Strasburg's blenny), Istiblennius zebra (zebra blenny, pao'o), Plagiotremus ewaensis (Ewa blenny), Plagiotremus goslinei (scaleeating blenny), Callionymus caeruleonotatus (bluespotted dragonet), Callionymus comptus (ornamented dragonet), Callionymus decoratus (longtail dragonet), Draculo pogognathus (no common name), Synchiropus hawaiiensis (no common name), Synchiropus kinmeiensis (no common name), Cabillus caudimacula (no common name), Eviota rubra (no common name), Eviota susanae (no common name), Oxyurichthys heisei (ribbon goby), Oxyurichthys lonchotus (no common name), Pleurosicya larsonae (no common name), Psilogobius mainlandi (Mainland's goby), Enneapterygius atriceps (Hawaiian Triplefin), Antennarius commerson (Commerson's frogfish), Caracanthus typicus (Hawaiian orbicular velvetfish), Pterois sphex (Hawaiian Hawaiʻi's State Wildlife Action Plan October 1, 2025 turkeyfish, nohu pinao), Scorpaena pele (no common name), Scorpaenopsis altirostris (no common name), Scorpaenopsis brevifrons (shortnose scorpionfish), Scorpaenopsis cacopsis (titan scorpionfish, nohu), Scorpaenopsis pluralis (no common name), Synodus falcatus (no common name), and Synodus janus (no common name). Synchiropus hawaiiensis and Synchiropus kinmeiensis may be the same species. Bruce Mundy (National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS)) reports that Jack Randall 
(Bishop Museum)
 will publish a manuscript reporting that S. janus is a junior synonym of S. falcatus so these are probably just a single species.

## Cryptic Reef Fishes

DISTRIBUTION: Distributed throughout the Hawaiian Islands, primarily in shallow reef habitats and tide pools. Enchelyurus occurs from O'ahu to Lisianski. Entomacrodus strasburgi occurs from Moloka'i to O'ahu. Zebra blennies occur from Hawai'i Island to Lisianski. The scale-eating blenny occurs from the island of Hawai'i to Pearl and Hermes Atoll. Bluespotted dragonets occur in the main islands only. Ornameneted dragonet, Mainland's goby, and Scorpaena pele have been found from Maui to O'ahu. The longtail dragonet is found from Maui to Pearl and Hermes Atoll. Draculo has been found from Moloka'i to Kaua'i. Synchiropus hawaiiensis has been found from Maui to Moloka'i. Synchiropus kinmeiensis has been collected from Maro Reef through Kure Atoll and the Emperor Seamounts. Cabillus, the two Eviota species, and Pleurosicya have only been found off O'ahu. The ribbon goby is found off Lāna'i and Moloka'i.
Oxyurichthys lonchotus has been collected from Hawai'i Island to O'ahu. Hawaiian orbicular velvetfish have been found from O'ahu through Midway Atoll. Scorpaenopsis altirostris is found from the island of Hawai'i to Moloka'i. Scorpaenopsis pluralis is known only from the holotype from near Laysan. Synodus falcatus has been found from Moloka'i through Laysan Island. Synodus janus is only known from the holotype collected off the island of Hawai'i. All the other species occur throughout the Hawaiian Islands.

## ABUNDANCE:

Common but underreported in surveys due to their small size and hidden habitats.The shallow water species are surveyed for in surveys of coral reef fishes in the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (NMWHI), both by NMFS and the Division of Aquatic Resources and data are available online. Nohu pinao (Hawaiian turkeyfish) and titan scorpionfish may have declined from historic levels and a few hundred pounds of titan scorpionfish are reported in State commercial catch data each year.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

All species except bluespotted dragonet, the two Synchiropus species, ribbon goby, Synodus falcatus, Scorpaena pele, and Scorpaenopsis altirostris can be found in shallow water depths. Callionymus coeruleonotatus is found in depths over 45 meters (150 feet), Oxyurichthys heisei, the Synchiropus species and Scorpaenopsis altirostris and Scorpaenopsis pluralis occur over 90 meters (300 feet) deep, S. falcatus has only been found in depths greater than 30 meters (100 feet), and Scorpaena pele has been found deeper than 150 meters (500 feet). 'Upāpalu (spotted cardinalfish) occurs in caves during the day and feeds nocturnally over a wider area. The gargantuan blenny lives on rocky shores exposed to wave action. Zebra blennies and the Entomacrodus species live in shallow, rocky surge zones and can even leap from pool to pool. Enchelyurus occupies dead coral heads. Most callionymids, Cabillus, Oxyurichthys lonchotus, and the lizardfishes occur in sandy or muddy habitats. The two Eviota species have been found around Kāne'ohe Bay, E. rubra from deeper spur and groove and E.

 susanae from shallow waters inside the bay. The Hawaiian orbicular velvetfish occurs among the branches of live coral. The scorpionfishes are often found hidden or under ledges. The rest are found throughout coral reef habitats.

## THREATS:

• Habitat Loss: Coral reef destruction from human activities and climate change.
• Pollution: Sedimentation and nutrient runoff reduce habitat quality.
• Invasive Species: Competition with invasive algae and fish species.
• Climate Change: Ocean warming and acidification impact reef structures and ecosystems.
• Lack of Awareness: Limited recognition of their ecological importance.
• Only a few of these species are prized by aquarists. These are gargantuan blenny, zebra blenny, Commerson's frogfish, Hawaiian orbicular velvetfish, and nohu pinao (Hawaiian turkeyfish); • Titan scorpionfish are fished commercially and recreationally; • Many species have restricted ranges within the State (see above).

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The goals of conservation actions are to not only protect current populations, but to also establish further populations to reduce the risk of extinction. Commercial licenses are required for aquarium collectors. In addition to common statewide and island conservation actions, specific actions include:
• Reef Protection: Implement marine protected areas to safeguard reef habitats.
• Habitat Restoration: Promote coral restoration projects and remove invasive species.
• Pollution Control: Mitigate land-based sources of pollution through better watershed management. • Public Education: Raise awareness about the importance of cryptic reef fishes in ecosystem health. • Research Support: Fund studies to improve understanding of these species.

## MONITORING:

• Population Surveys: Use specialized methods such as cryptic fish surveys and baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS). • Habitat Assessment: Monitor reef condition and structural complexity.
• Citizen Science: Engage divers and snorkelers in observing and reporting sightings.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

• Species Identification: Catalog cryptic species and their roles in reef ecosystems.
• Ecological Roles: Study their contributions to algae control, nutrient cycling, and food webs.
• Resilience Studies: Assess their adaptability to changing environmental conditions.
• Threat Impact: Investigate specific threats like invasive species and microplastics.
• Conservation Value: Highlight their ecological importance in reef conservation strategies.
• Support aquaculture research to develop captive breeding for species used in the aquarium trad

Freshwater eels migrate between marine and freshwater environments for reproduction, while moray eels are reef-dwelling predators. Both groups are crucial components of aquatic ecosystems. Morays and snake eels (ophicthids) are carnivores of fishes and invertebrates. Morays are often nocturnal. Hawaiian garden eel (Gorgasia) is a planktivore. Other conger eels are largely nocturnal carnivores. Many moray eels are hermaphrodites of one form or another. The species common names and Hawaiian names are Anarchias sp. (no common name), Enchelycore pardalis (dragon eel, puhi-kauila), Gymnothorax nuttingi (Nutting's moray), Gymnothorax polyspondylus (many-vertebrate moray), Gymnothorax steindachneri (Steindachner's moray, puhi), Callechelys lutea (yellow-spotted snake eel, puhi), Ichthyapus platyrhychus (no common name), Ophichthus fowleri (Fowler's snake eel), Ophichthus kunaloa (nom common name), Scolecenchelys phuioilo (no common name), Acromycter alcocki (no common name), Bathycongrus aequorea (no common name), and Gorgasia hawaiiensis (Hawaiian garden eel, puhi). DISTRIBUTION: The many-vertebrate moray has been found off O'ahu only. Steindachner's moray has been found from O'ahu through the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (NWHI). Stable for some species, declining for others due to habitat loss and overfishing. The shallow water species are surveyed for in surveys of coral reef fishes in the Main and NWHI, both by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Division of Aquatic Resources and data are available online.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

All species except Nutting's moray, manyvertebrate moray, Ophichthus kunaloa, Scolecenchelys, Acromycter, and Bathycongrus are found in shallow water. Nutting's moray is found deeper than 110 meters (350 feet), the many-vertebrate moray was collected deeper than 180 meters (600 feet), and Ophichthus kunaloa and Scolecenchelys puhioilo are collected only greater than 210 meters (700 feet) deep. Acromycter and Bathycongrus have been collected only deeper than 300 meters (1,000 feet). Steindachner's moray is only found deeper than 30 meters (100 feet) in the main islands. Snake eels and Hawaiian garden eels occur in sandy habitat. The rest are found throughout coral reef habitats. Puhi-kauila (dragon eel) is more common in the NWHI.

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

Seahorses and pipefish are small, elongated fishes with bony armor and unique appearances. Seahorses have prehensile tails for gripping, while pipefish are slender and adapted for camouflage in seagrass and algae. These species all share a body structure made of bony rings. The pipefishes and seahorses have sex-role reversal where the males accept and guard eggs in internal pouches or on their skin until the young hatch. This takes from ten to 50 days. They are predators that feed mostly on small crustaceans. The Hawaiian sea moth is a deeper water species. Redstripe pipefish often occur in small groups of mixed age. They have also been observed cleaning other fishes. Fisher's seahorse is apparently pelagic, attaching to floating algae. All species are less than 30 centimeters (one foot) in length and mostly half of that.
DISTRIBUTION: Hawaiian sea moths and Edmondson's pipefish are found statewide. Ball's pipefish has been found from O'ahu to Kaua'i. The redstripe pipefish has only been found from the island of Hawai'i to O'ahu. Fisher's seahorse is found from Maui to the island of Hawai'i but may be more widespread. The spiny seahorse is only known from a specimen from Maui. The Yellow seahorse is found in the main islands and up to Necker Island.

## ABUNDANCE:

Difficult to estimate due to cryptic nature and habitat specificity. These species (except the deep Hawaiian sea moths) are looked for in surveys of coral reef fishes in the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, both by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Division of Aquatic Resources. A recent survey in the main islands found that seahorses and pipefishes were rare.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

Preferred habitat is shallow, vegetated marine environments such as seagrass beds, coral rubble, and mangroves. Seahorses use plants to anchor themselves by their tails. Pipefishes often use the area under ledges. They all occur in moderately shallow water, except the sea moth which occurs in water over 60 meters (200 feet) deep, often in algal beds. Juvenile Hawaiian sea moths can be found in shallow water.
Edmondson's pipefish can often be found in tidepools. The Yellow seahorse can be found in brackish waters.

## THREATS:

• Habitat Loss: Destruction of seagrass beds and coastal habitats.
• Overharvesting: Collection for aquarium trade and traditional medicine. These species are prized by aquarists, and seahorses are used in some Asian cultures for medicinal and other purposes. Aquaculture research collection may also be a threat • Pollution: Sedimentation and chemical runoff affecting water quality.
• Climate Change: Ocean warming and acidification threatening habitat and prey availability.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The goals of conservation actions are to not only protect current populations, but to also establish further populations to reduce the risk of extinction. Seahorses are listed in CITES Appendix II and pipefishes are being considered for such
Hawaiʻi's State Wildlife Action Plan October 1, 2025
protection. Commercial licenses are required for aquarium collectors. In addition to common state-wide and island conservation actions, specific actions include:

• Trade Regulation: Implement sustainable practices under CITES regulations.
• Community Involvement: Engage local communities in conservation efforts.
• Pollution Control: Reduce coastal runoff and improve water quality management.

## MONITORING:

• Population Surveys: Use diver and snorkeler observations to assess population trends.
• Habitat Assessments: Monitor the health of seagrass beds and associated ecosystems.
• Trade Data: Track export/import records for aquarium species.
• Climate Impact Studies: Analyze the effects of changing ocean conditions on species distribution.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

• Habitat Use: Study preferences for specific habitats and ecological roles.
• Reproductive Biology: Understand breeding and lifecycle dynamics.
• Climate Resilience: Evaluate adaptive capacity to ocean changes.
• Conservation Techniques: Develop aquaculture and restoration methods for seahorses and pipefish.

LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT: Manta rays can be predictably found off parts of the west coast of Hawai'i Island, and throughout the reef areas on all the main Hawaiian islands. Oceanic manta rays are wide ranging and found further offshore. Not much is currently known about their key habitats in Hawaiian waters. DAR and other partner organizations are currently studying oceanic manta rays to learn more about their key habitats and population dynamics.
THREATS: These species have slow growth rates and low fecundity that limit their recovery from threats.
• Overfishing. Targeted for gill rakers internationally.
• Bycatch. Incidental entanglement in fishing gear, anchor/mooring lines.
• Vessel Strikes. Incidental collisions with mantas surface feeding.
• Habitat Degradation. Loss of coastal habitat, like reefs.
• Climate Change. Altered ocean temperatures and acidification impacting ecosystems.
• Pollution. Bioaccumulation of toxins from plastics and heavy metals.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The State proposes the following conservation actions specific to oceanic and reef manta rays:
• Reducing marine debris and pollutants in the marine environment.
• Reducing fishery interactions through education and outreach campaigns, including gear modifications as well as de-hooking techniques. • Collaborating with local organizations working on manta tracking, identifying, conservation and education. • Collaborate on the implementation of the NMFS Recovery Plan.

## MONITORING:

The State proposes the following monitoring actions specific to oceanic and reef manta rays:
• Monitoring abundance and distribution of mantas in Hawaiian waters.
• Monitoring entanglement and fisheries bycatch.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

The State proposes the following research priorities specific to oceanic and reef manta rays:
• Performing stock assessments to gather population information.
• Researching the oceanic whitetip social structure.

## ABUNDANCE:

Hawaiian Mussel (Nahawele li'i li'i):

## Marine Invertebrates

Black & Wire Corals 

## Grand Black Coral

Antipathes grandis 

## Hawaiian Black Coral

Antipathes griggi Cirrhipathes anguina is native but not exclusive to Hawaiʻi.

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

Black and wire corals (Antipatharia) are tree-like or stick-like cnidarians with dark brown skeletons covered in small spines. Live colonies may appear rusty brown, orange, yellow, green, or white due to the polyps' colors and may fluoresce under certain conditions. These corals play a crucial ecological role by providing food and shelter for various marine life, including fishes, mollusks, crustaceans, and commensal organisms like gobies and shrimps.
• Antipathes grandis: Flexible branching structure with high commercial value.
• Antipathes griggi: Often associated with rare fishes, such as the longnose hawkfish (Oxycirrhites typus) and Tinker's butterflyfish (Chaetodon tinkeri). • Cirrhipathes anguina: Polyps present on all sides of the stick-like coral. Often hosts commensal species like wire coral gobies and shrimps.
Antipatharians have long played a role in Hawaiian cultural traditions and marine ecosystems. These ancient and slow-growing organisms provide essential habitats for symbiotic species and contribute to the biodiversity of Hawaiʻi's deep reefs. Protecting these corals ensures the health of Hawaiʻi's underwater ecosystems for future generations while preserving the natural heritage of these islands.
DISTRIBUTION: Black and wire corals are found along current-swept reefs and drop-offs across the Hawaiian Archipelago. While some species, such as Antipathes griggi, are accessible to divers in shallow waters, others, like Antipathes grandis, are restricted to depths typically explored by submersibles.

## THREATS

• Harvesting: Antipathes grandis has been extensively harvested for jewelry, significantly reducing populations. • Habitat Degradation: Pollution and climate change threaten reef health and the habitats where these corals thrive. CONSERVATION ACTIONS: Conservation efforts include protecting existing populations through fishing regulations, law enforcement, and public education. These efforts aim to ensure that the population remains healthy and sustainable for future generations. Similar to Ula poni, conservation efforts for Ula focus on enforcing fishing regulations and protecting their habitat from further destruction. Public education and sustainable fisheries management are key to ensuring their future.

## MONITORING:

Ongoing population monitoring helps assess the effectiveness of current fishing regulations and conservation measures.
Monitoring the populations of Ula is essential for understanding the impacts of fishing practices and the effectiveness of conservation efforts.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

• Larval Distribution: Further study of larval movement and distribution is essential to understanding population dynamics. • Population Dynamics: Research is needed to better understand the factors affecting the population size, such as fishing pressures and habitat changes.
Both species of spiny lobsters are important components of their ecosystems and face significant challenges due to human activities, especially overfishing and habitat destruction. Conservation actions, such as regulated fishing seasons, habitat protection, and public education, are crucial for maintaining healthy populations of these species for future generations.

## DISTRIBUTION:

All species occur throughout Hawai'i. The chocolate-chip sea cucumber can be found in the Main Hawaiian Islands (MHI) and the North Western Hawaiian Islands (NWHI).

## ABUNDANCE: Unknown

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

The spear urchin and the Hawaiian thorny urchin are found in deeper depth beyond scuba range, whereas the other urchins are found within scuba range depths (up to 130 feet). Thomas's sea urchin primarily is found in deeper waters within scuba range and as shallow as 9 meters (30 feet) and stays under coral slabs and in crevices during the day. The Glass-spined urchins live on rocky substrates from approximately 6 to over 46 meters (20 to over 150 feet). Small fine spined urchins are most often found under stones, while larger ones in caves and crevices. Hawaiian lovenia lives in the sand. Both species of the endemic sea stars are uncommon in scuba depths and live on rocky substrates. M. fisheri primary habitat is on cave ceilings and walls. The chocolate chip and the Hawaiian spiny sea cucumbers are found out in the open beside coral reefs in sand and rubble. The Hawaiian spiny sea cucumbers can also be found on steep slopes from approximately 15 to 46 meters (50 to 150 feet). Hawaiian yellow-tip sea cucumbers prefer areas under stones during the day.

## SPECIES INFORMATION:

The species of nudibranchs listed, including Aldisa pikokai (pitted nudibranch), Ardeadoris scottjohnsoni (Scott Johnson's nudibranch), Chromodoris vibrata (trembling nudibranch), Glossodoris poliahu (snow goddess nudibranch), Halgerda terramtuentis (gold lace nudibranch), Hypselodoris andersoni (Anderson's nudibranch), Melibe megaceras, Peltodoris fellowsi (Fellow's nudibranch), and Sclerodoris paliensis (pali nudibranch), are carnivores that feed on a range of organisms such as sponges, hydroids, corals, and even other nudibranchs. The pitted nudibranch is the only nocturnal feeder among them. All species are hermaphroditic and mate through mutual insemination. They lay their eggs in coiled ribbons, which hatch into trochophore larvae. These larvae eventually develop into planktonic veligers and lose their shell once they settle. Most nudibranchs have a lifespan of less than a year. Notably, nudibranchs are usually toxic due to the recycling of toxins from their prey, although they do not produce their own toxins.

## DISTRIBUTION:

Most of the species are found throughout the Hawaiian archipelago. However, the gold lace nudibranch (Halgerda terramtuentis) is restricted to the Main Hawaiian Islands.

## ABUNDANCE:

The snow goddess nudibranch (Glossodoris poliahu) is uncommon. There is limited quantitative data regarding abundance trends for the other species.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

• Aldisa pikokai (pitted nudibranch) prefers waters from 2 to 9 meters (6 to 30 feet), though it can be found up to 24 meters (80 feet) deep, favoring areas with stones and crevices. ranging from 5 to 30 meters (15 to 100 feet).
• Hypselodoris andersoni (Anderson's nudibranch) inhabits caves and under overhangs on exposed rocky shores from 5 to 18 meters (15 to 60 feet), occasionally in shallower waters of harbors and boat channels, where they often live on the yellow sponge Luffariella metachromia.
• Peltodoris fellowsi (Fellow's nudibranch) is found near cave entrances in waters from 6 to 15 meters (20 to 50 feet) or deeper and typically resides on sponges. • Sclerodoris paliensis (pali nudibranch) is found in waters from 2 to 6 meters (6 to 20 feet) deep. Specific habitat data for the other species has not been provided.

## THREATS:

The aquarium trade targets certain species, including the gold lace, Fellow's, and pali nudibranchs.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The primary goals of conservation actions include not only protecting existing populations but also establishing new populations to reduce the risk of extinction. Specific actions include:
• Maintaining healthy populations through appropriate aquarium fishing regulations, enforcement, and education.

## MONITORING:

Surveys for populations and distribution in known and potential habitats should continue.

## RESEARCH PRIORITIES:

• Improve understanding of factors affecting the population sizes and distributions of these species.

They grow to a maximum mantle length of 3.5 centimeters and live between three to ten months. Mūhe'e have limited diurnal activity as they bury themselves in the sand during the day. While foraging for shrimp or worms in the water column on moonlit nights, they use counterillumination to camouflage themselves from potential predators on the seafloor. They do this with the help of the luminescent symbiont bacteria, Vibrio fischeri, that resides in a light organ within its mantle cavity. Both the he'e and the Hawaiian short-arm sand octopus have the innate ability to camouflage themselves from predators by changing the color of their skin to match their environment. The Hawaiian short-arm sand octopus is also highly skilled at burrowing into the sand as a way of camouflage. Little is recorded of the habits of he'e and the Hawaiian short-arm sand octopus.
DISTRIBUTION: All three cephalopod species are found throughout the Hawaiian Islands.

## ABUNDANCE:

Not known for any of the three species.

## LOCATION AND CONDITION OF KEY HABITAT:

The primary habitat of he'e is rocky substrate or shallow reef flats in waters ranging from approximately five to nine meters (15 to 30 feet) deep, however they can be found at any depth. The primary habitat of the Hawaiian short-arm sand octopus are sandy substrates within shallow coastal waters ranging from 1-80 meters in depth. Mūhe'e can be found in shallow waters on either sand or mud flats. This habitat is important to mūhe'e because it uses the substrate during the day to burrow, and its main prey is found in this area. The habitat of mūhe'e is in decline, especially in areas like Kāne'ohe Bay, O'ahu where the bay is affected by urbanization and sedimentation.

## THREATS:

• Habitat degradation is the primary threat to the mūhe'e and a concern for the Hawaiian short-arm sand octopus and he'e as well. Habitat degradation results from urbanization, runoff, and sedimentation. These threats not only alter its habitat but may negatively affect prey availability; • Aquarium and research fishing pressure is a concern for mūhe'e;
• Recreational collectors create fishing pressure for he'e and the Hawaiian short-arm sand octopus.

## CONSERVATION ACTIONS:

The goals of conservation actions are to not only protect current populations, but to also establish further populations to reduce the risk of extinction. In addition to common state-wide and island conservation actions, specific actions include:
• Restore and maintain habitat, especially for mūhe'e;
• Cooperate with other agencies to minimize pollution in areas such as Kāne'ohe Bay;
• Enforce regulations and education for aquarium trade and recreational collectors.

## 7-11 or Blood-Spot Crab Carpilius maculatus

A striking crab with red spots resembling the pattern of dice, hence its nickname "7-11 crab." Its carapace can grow up to 6 inches in width. Found in rocky tidepools and coral reef areas. Although it is widespread throughout the Indo-Pacific, it is also found in Hawai'i. It is a nocturnal omnivore, feeding on algae, small invertebrates, and organic matter.

## Sleepy Sponge Crab Tumidodromia dromia

An uncommon species found under ledges and in caverns. This crab uses its hind legs to hold sponges, which serve as camouflage and protection. Its carapace can grow up to 8 inches wide, making it one of the largest crabs in the region. It is believed to be poisonous and is also known as the largest sponge crab in the world. Found in Hawai'i and the Indo-Pacific.

## Hawaiian Pom-Pom Crab Lybia edmondsoni

A fascinating crab known for carrying venomous anemones (Triactis producta) in its claws as both a defense mechanism and a tool for capturing prey. Its carapace reaches a width of 1/2 inch. Occasional under rocks in shallow waters, it is endemic to Hawai'i. Related to the Indo-Pacific Lybia tessellata.

## Button Crab Pseudopalicus oahuensis

An uncommon crab found on reefs at night, identifiable by its hind legs lined with long hair that aids in camouflage. Carapace width attains1 inch. Distributed across Hawai'i and the Indo-Pacific. No previous scientific name recorded.
